1.	Has the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources made any statements in the past year about the development of skiing in the maritime national parks?
2.	If so, when, where, and to what effect?
3.	At the present time, how much skiing takes place in the national parks located in Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I will answer parts 1, 2, and 3 together, Mr. Speaker.
At the present time, little or no skiing takes place in the national park located in Nova Scotia. However, within the past year I have received representations from the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Muir), about the possibility of developing some organized skiing facilities in the Cape Breton Highlands national park. Similar representations have been received from the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) with respect to Fundy national park in New Brunswick. I have also held discussions with 26207-1-79
interested individuals in the areas concerned and with representatives of the local chambers of commerce.
Following these representations I made arrangements for an expert, Mr. Franz Baier, to understake a technical survey of the skiing development potential of these national parks. Mr. Baier has completed his assessment and has submitted a report, which is now being studied by the officers of my department.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: USE OP NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN EVENT OF WAR
speechtext:
I should like to ask the Prime

Minister whether he would care to comment on a press report to the effect that he indicated in Edmonton on Saturday last that if war broke out Canadian forces would be armed with nuclear weapons.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: USE OP NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN EVENT OF WAR
speechtext: The statement I made the other day in no way represented a change of viewpoint on the part of the government of this country, and I hope the Leader of the Opposition would agree that if war came, should nuclear weapons be used against us Canadian troops participating should not be denied the right to use nuclear weapons.

subtopic: USE OP NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN EVENT OF WAR
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: USE OP NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN EVENT OF WAR
speechtext:
What I stated was but a repetition of what has been said on previous occasions. I would simply refer the house to what I stated on November 24, 1960, when speaking to the Canadian club of Ottawa; on August 15, 1961, when speaking in Halifax to the Canadian Weekly Newspapers Association; and again, on October 6, 1961 when Dr. Thomson and those associated with him in the Canadian committee for the control of radiation hazards made representations to the government.
We take the stand that in the interests of disarmament everything must be done to assure success if it can be attained, and that the nuclear family should not be increased so long as there is any possibility of disarmament among the nations of the world. That has been our view throughout; that was the reason for our vote on the Swedish resolution which came before the United Nations.

subtopic: USE OP NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN EVENT OF WAR
speechtext: In view of what the Prime Minister has said, to the effect that nuclear arms would be in the hands of Canadian forces if war broke out and nuclear arms were used against them-I think I am right in my interpretation of what the right hon. gentleman said-may I ask whether such weapons would be in the hands of Canadian forces before the outbreak of war?

subtopic: USE OP NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN EVENT OF WAR
speechtext: I referred to the outbreak of war and said that in the event that nuclear war was launched, nuclear weapons should be placed in the possession of Canadians.

subtopic: USE OP NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN EVENT OF WAR
speechtext:
May I ask a
supplementary question. Could these weapons be used without the approval of the United States authorities?

subtopic: USE OP NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN EVENT OF WAR
speechtext:
Our views in that regard were set forth at length in February, 1959. At that time I said-and I am simply summarizing the remarks I made in the house-that in the event we should decide to make nuclear weapons available it would be necessary to have joint control on the part of Canada and

the United States. That attitude, of course, has not been generally accepted. If I understand the Leader of the Opposition aright, some weeks ago he took the stand that he objected at any time to joint control, but he would be willing to have the United States store nuclear warheads in Canada.
That view we have never held. Our view is that at the moment this is hypothetical and will continue to be so as long as disarmament is to the fore. But should it be decided in the light of Canadian armament needs and defence responsibility that nuclear weapons are to be had at any time, joint control is of the essence of the stand we have taken.

subtopic: USE OP NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN EVENT OF WAR
speechtext: It is not possible, of course, in a question to remove the misunderstanding which the Prime Minister has created about my position in this matter. I ask the Prime Minister, therefore, this question. In view of the constitutional position of the United States, and in view of recent statements of the President of that country, how does the Prime Minister propose to bring about this joint control?

subtopic: USE OP NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN EVENT OF WAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman knows very well that so long as the law of the United States is as it is at present, joint control is impossible.

subtopic: USE OP NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN EVENT OF WAR
speechtext: Then we cannot have the weapons.

subtopic: USE OP NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN EVENT OF WAR
speechtext: What I have stated is exactly the position of affairs. We have stated that until the United States makes joint control available, we do not intend to go further than we have unless war breaks out, at which time we hope to have available to Canadians the necessary nuclear weapons. That is much clearer than the evasive policy of the Leader of the Opposition.

speechtext:

It will be the task of the west in the months ahead to seek through negotiation the achievement of the Latin expression which the hon. gentleman used, a modus vivendi which will respect the essential interests both of the west and of the U.S.S.R. in the Berlin problem. Mr. Speaker, this is a traditional opportunity for those of us in opposition to raise some matters of great importance dealing with the Canadian economy. I therefore take that opportunity today in order to deal with what will be the theme in the next election and what is the greatest issue before the people today. The Prime Minister has suggested several possible themes for the next general election such as free enterprise versus socialism, senate reform and things of that nature. This is, of course, an attempt to blur and becloud the basic issues before the country, in an attempt to divert people's attention from the shortcomings of this government in meeting emerging problems.

Alleged Lack of Economic Growth
I cannot during this debate discuss all the essential problems such as social security and national unity which will have to be faced and solved soon. Apart from the threat to world peace, however, the paramount issue is the lack of economic growth, the nation's nearly stagnant economy. Without adequate and planned growth a relatively large number of our Canadian workers will remain unemployed, the farmers will accumulate surpluses, private enterprise will continue in hesitancy; municipalities will deteriorate through being unable to improve their local services, and other levels of government will find it increasingly difficult to extend our social security system to other areas of collective risks. In other words, economic growth is essential not only to a rising standard of living but also to the progress and improvement of all the other aspects of our national life.
Economic growth therefore must be the key domestic issue of the next general election. In the economic debate that has taken place in Canada in recent years the Liberal party has taken and is taking a realistic and responsible attitude. We are saying that the Canadian economy has not grown as it should have grown since 1957, and that the government has failed to take appropriate action to correct the situation. We in contrast are putting forward a concrete program to promote rapid and balanced growth.
What is the attitude of this Conservative government? They make the preposterous claim that the Liberal party is selling Canada short when it underlines the lack of economic growth. They say that Canadians never had it so good, and they apparently do not propose to do anything except to publicize their meagre accomplishments. This charge that we on this side are selling Canada short reminds me of another economic debate which took place during the last presidential campaign in the United States, and of Mr. Nixon's position in that debate as described by Meg Greenfield in an article entitled "The Prose of Richard M. Nixon" which appeared in The Reporter on September 29, 1960. This is what she had to say:
The identification of his opponents with communism is generally considered to be a chapter from Nixon's past. In not very subtle ways, however, he has managed to assert throughout the last two years that those who have criticized him or the Eisenhower administration or the Republican party on matters ranging from the economy to national defence have not in fact attacked those policies but have attacked America itself. The implication is either that they have suggested we adopt a communist system, or, when this won't do, that they have not criticized a policy but a basic American institution. "It's time to stop selling America short" appears to be the grand theme of


his campaign for the presidency, suggesting as it does some unspecific deficiency of patriotism in his opponents.
That surely has a familiar ring to hon. members of this house. I am quite sure that the tactics used by Mr. Nixon in the United States will not be more successful in Canada, as Canadians know too well their own economic difficulties to accept the rosy picture that the Conservatives are attempting to present to them.
Let us now look at the facts, Mr. Speaker. I might remind hon. members, if they do not choose to listen, that I am in that rather special category in which I have all day to speak.
Oh, oh.
Oh, no; have mercy on us.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member has indicated her proper position when she says she has all day to speak. I trust that those who are listening will give their early attention to what she has to say.

Let us look at the facts, Mr. Speaker. The Conservatives claim that our economic troubles are over simply because the Canadian economy is going through another cyclical upswing in business. There is nothing exceptional about the present recovery. It is due to the normal pattern of change in inventories, and is just another phase of the short cycle.
In March, 1961 my leader was the first in this house to say that the 1960 recession was over because the process of inventory liquidation was then completed. In the latter part of 1961 economic conditions began to improve, and several experts forecast an increase of about 6 per cent in the gross national product at market prices for 1962. This increase would be about the same as that in 1959, when unemployment remained at an average rate of 6 per cent. This is certainly nothing to boast about for a period of peak activity.
Indeed, the experts also predict that another recession will begin at the end of 1962 or at the beginning of 1963. Again this is the normal pattern of the short cycle. Recessions tend to appear every three years: in 1954, in 1957, and in 1960. It is quite normal, therefore, to expect the beginning of another one during the next fiscal year. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this is the appropriate time for the government to anticipate such an unfortunate event and prepare plans now to cope with it before it comes. This is exactly what President Kennedy is doing in the United States.
The Leader of the Opposition, it may be recalled, made the same suggestion to the government on April 12, 1960, in this house

when he warned that the Canadian economy was on the eve of another recession. The government did not accept his warning then, and it blindly refused to plan accordingly. As a matter of fact, here is what the Minister of Finance had to say at that time as found at page 3167 of Hansard of April 12, 1960:
The Leader of the Opposition was so anxious this afternoon to get everybody talking recession with him that he was in effect asking the Minister of Finance what preparations he was making for the next recession. The best preparation that can be made for the next recession is to continue the present government in office.
He continued:
That is the surest guarantee of avoiding a recession.
The Minister of Finance was wrong again. The recession began during the second quarter of 1960, but the government did not even recognize its existence before the very end of that year. It did not recognize the problem of increasing unemployment. As a matter of fact one of the ministers of the crown, as I recall, said that it would melt with the snow.
The Minister of Finance.

Furthermore, the government even avoided the use of the word in the throne speech debate of November, 1960. I hope that same mistake will not be made this time, and that the Minister of Finance will be realistic enough to anticipate this new danger and act accordingly. I hope that this time he will do more than just sit passively and watch it happen.
Moreover, this current recovery is not without its weaknesses. I do not see how we can be satisfied with the present economic situation when, at a cyclical peak, the rate of unemployment is 8.5 per cent, and when this very poor result has been obtained because of our labour force remaining stable, a factor which is quite abnormal. I have been truly shocked since the opening of this parliament to see the self-satisfaction of the government over the problem of unemployment, as though the problem no longer existed, although almost half a million Canadians still remain unemployed.
The condition of Canadian agriculture is certainly not bright. The dairy industry, which is so important in eastern Canada, is in deep difficulties. This can best be illustrated by the tremendous butter surplus that has been accumulating in recent years. There were widespread rumours last year that the government would announce a new policy, but as usual it has not dared to come to grips with the issue. The Prime Minister has announced instead that the dairy industry
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth will have to wait until May for a policy statement. Meanwhile it has to live under conditions of complete uncertainty as to its immediate future.
In the prairie provinces, Mr. Speaker, net farm income declined by about 45 per cent in 1961 compared with 1960, according to the most recent figures published by the dominion bureau of statistics. This tragic decline was caused by the reduction in production of grain crops in 1961 brought about by the terrible losses of last summer's drought, and the consequent drop in the year end inventories of grain on farms. We are also told that the outlook for 1962 is not very bright because of a lack of soil moisture, and that the supplies as at January 1 of this year were 465.3 million bushels compared with 745.9 million last year. Our wheat surplus may soon be completely eliminated, but it will not be to the advantage of Canadian wheat producers. We are committed to new sales abroad at a time when we may not be able to produce enough to fulfil our traditional commitments.
The current mild and temporary recovery reveals the more fundamental weaknesses of the Canadian economy. When we look at our long term situation it becomes evident that since 1956 our economy has simply failed to grow. This lack of growth appears clearly when we compare recent figures with the previous period and with the requirements of full employment. You say, what is the evidence? From 1950 to 1956 the average annual increase in our gross national product in constant dollars was 6 per cent. From 1957 to 1961 it has been 1.5 per cent. In 1956, compared with 1950, the volume of our gross national product on a per capita basis had increased by 22 per cent; but in 1961, compared with 1956, it had declined by more than 4 per cent.
From 1950 to 1957 total capital expenditures in constant dollars increased by 62 per cent, but since 1957 they have declined by 12 per cent. During these last self-same five years business capital expenditures in constant dollars have declined by almost 25 per cent. From 1950 to 1956 the average rate of unemployment was 3 per cent. Since 1957 it has exceeded 6 per cent. The average level of unemployment in 1961 was the highest in the post-war period, 7.2 per cent, in spite of the fact that net immigration estimated at 13,000-that is, only 13,000 more people coming into the country than those going out of it-was at its lowest post-war level.
Those are the basic facts which describe the long term situation of the Canadian economy. It is not a rosy picture, but it is

Alleged Lack of Economic Growth a true picture. This is not glooming and dooming; this is a responsible discussion of the facts.
There are two other important aspects of this situation which must be mentioned. First, our export trade which is so vital to us is going through a revolutionary period. More than 50 per cent of the increase in our trade went to communist countries in the first nine months of 1961. This is a new but very unstable trade diversion. No one can tell how long such markets will continue. Moreover, the emergence of new trade blocs represents a challenge which the government is still refusing to face. The government, rather than embracing the idea of such potentially great trade developments, has hung back and consistently played the obstructionist. Second, it has been estimated that we will have to have one million additional new jobs in Canada during the first half of the 1960's in order to achieve reasonable levels of employment.
Since the present government came into office our economy has slowed down. While the government lauds itself because more people are employed, it suppresses any real discussion of the fact that we are barely holding our own and creating nowhere near sufficient jobs to take care of the present, much less the future. The government would have us believe that they are doing everything possible to alleviate unemployment, and that since nothing more can be done the whole matter might better be ignored. It has attempted to fix responsibility for this situation upon us, upon a prior administration. Who can forget the biggest single group in Canada who were suddenly thrust out of work in 1958 at the instance of this government, that skilled technical team at Malton building the Arrow and the Orenda engine, some 16,000 Canadians who at one blow were placed out of work? With that same blow Canada suffered the loss of a complex of highly skilled people such as we had never before put together and may never again. The government cast them away. Most of them left for the United States, which realizes the necessity for the development of such a force of scientists and technicians. This is what an editorial in the February issue of Aircraft magazine has to say, speaking of a young man who was part of the Avro team:
James Chamberlin is a Canadian now living and working in the United States. It is ironical that three years alter his departure from Canada his name may become nationally known. It is possible that with an election approaching the case of Jim Chamberlin may become a cause celebre, for he is a symbol of the growing export of brains that Canada has supplied to the United States in the last few years.

Mr. Chamberlin has recently been named by NASA as project manager for project Gemini. Project Gemini is the next major man in space project by the United States and involves putting two men in orbit in separate capsules which will rendezvous while in orbit. The fact that a man who has not even been in the United States long enough to qualify for citizenship would be assigned by NASA to manage a project which means so much to U.S. international prestige is an indication of the high regard with which he is held in U.S. scientific and engineering circles. Too bad Canada couldn't have held Jim Chamberlin and others like him.
When the Prime Minister asks, as he did in the past few days, whether we are to fight the next world war with bows and arrows, the people of the country at least know, even if they do not know whether a Bomarc without a warhead is equivalent to an unstrung bow, that we will not be fighting with Arrows, and they know who are responsible for that.
The cost to Canadians of the slowdown in our economic pace is $14 billion. That is the difference between our actual production in the last four and a half years and the production we would have had if the economic growth of previous years had continued. The cost is nearly $800 worth of goods and services for every person in the country. The cost for a family of four is over $3,000, and the loss has been getting bigger every year. In 1961 alone it was about $5 billion, that is $100 million a week or nearly $600,000 for every hour of the day and $10,000 for every minute. Worse still, the slowdown means a loss of 300,000 jobs for Canadians, extra jobs which would now exist if economic growth in this country had continued since 1957 as it was before.
Third, then, Mr. Speaker, the fiscal and monetary policies of this government have done nothing to assist and, indeed, much to harm economic development. May I quote from an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press of February 22, 1962:
In Toronto, the citadel of the Conservative party, the Globe and Mail demands an early budget and a full disclosure of the financial facts both for the enlightenment of the Canadian people and for the reassurance of foreigners since "in the last year or so Canada's credit and standing abroad have deteriorated. The heavy national deficit, the long delay in bringing down the 1961 budget, and the rancorous quarrel between the government and the former governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. James Coyne, have created doubts about our financial responsibility." Lacking an early budget, says the Globe and Mail, "the result could be a sharp decline in much needed foreign investment."
Those are strong words from a government supporter but the Montreal Gazette, Canada's oldest and most reliable Conservative organ, appears to be more alarmed than its Toronto contemporary. It says:
The present situation, when both federal and provincial governments are running up deficits and

debts cannot continue .. . Obviously everybody cannot go on spending above revenues indefinitely without the day of reckoning being terribly cruel.
These, then, are the costs of Canada's wasted years; the years of Tory talk instead of action, of mismanagement instead of purposeful government. As I said before, economic growth will be the key domestic issue during the next election campaign. This time the Conservatives will be judged not on a vision but on their record, a record of wasted years as compared with the period of progress and development during the former Liberal administration.
In contrast, we on this side of the house are presenting an over-all program designed to meet the new problems and the changes which have recently emerged. We recommend a new and freer trade policy. The Leader of the Opposition, Mr. Speaker, has been in the forefront of those proposing new trade alliances in free trade areas such as the Atlantic community. We have, in addition, special programs to help those domestic industries which will have to adjust to freer trade. There are many such which have been undertaken in the various E.C.M. countries.
If I may, I should like to cite some of the procedures which are used in the various countries. I should like to point out that we are well aware of the fact that freer trade might have an adverse effect on some of our domestic industries, but that same fear was widespread in European countries and did not materialize. The governments of those countries applied some differing types of solutions through their budgets and through governmental action to adjust their domestic industries to this new trading community.
In Italy, Mr. Speaker, there is something called the fund for the south, which grants credits to small and medium sized industries for construction of new plants and modernization of existing ones. These loans bear 3 per cent interest for 15 years and cover 70 per cent of the cost of the project. Most hon. members will know that the southern part of Italy is much less developed than the northern and more industrialized part. Tax concessions in that country are allowed on investments in specific areas including exemptions of income tax, turnover tax, corporate tax, registration and mortgage taxes. Material and machinery in these regions are exempted from customs duties. An exemption from corporate income tax on a maximum of 50 per cent of corporate profits is granted, provided the tax exempt portion is used for new investment or to reactivate industrial plants. Municipal governments may grant exemption from all or part of taxes, such as commodity tax, consumption and land taxes,
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth due to them up to August, 1967. Lands required for new industries may be expropriated and made available at their agricultural rather than their industrial value.
In the Netherlands certain regions have been designated as development areas. Special provisions apply to investments in these localities. Subsidies based on additional useful floor area of new factories provide up to one half the cost of purchasing industrial sites. To qualify an entrepreneur must agree in principle to employ a specified number of male employees. Up to one third of the cost of equipment can be written off at an accelerated rate. A company is allowed to deduct in any one year losses sustained in the six preceding years, and new industries may carry forward losses until they are completely absorbed by subsequent profits.
In Luxembourg the minister of finance is vested with power to extend substantial reductions in tax rates in order to attract new industries. Incentives take the form of accelerated depreciation, loans at low interest rates, direct subsidies for underindustrialized areas to promote the building of new plants, and lease-purchase schemes for industrial buildings.
In France, Mr. Speaker, some of these procedures were used. During the post-war period two modernization and equipment plans have been implemented. A third one is to become operative this year. Under it accelerated depreciation is allowed on a specific range of assets required for updating French plants. Companies can charge against taxable income the full amount of investment in companies and associations approved by the government whose functions are to assist members in modernization. Expenditure on scientific research is encouraged by an initial depreciation allowance of 50 per cent, and contributions to scientific organizations are allowable up to 2 per cent of turnover.
In Belgium state loans at reduced rates of interest are made available to industry through approved credit organizations, which in turn receive state subsidies and guarantees. Government built factories are sold or leased back to industries. Such locations are exempt from real estate taxes for five years. About 30 per cent of investments in industrial land, buildings and equipment can be written off against corporate taxes over three years. The capital gains tax does not apply to returns on investment in development areas.
In Germany most of the aid to distressed areas applies only to Berlin. However, enterprises situated on or near the eastern frontier are granted accelerated depreciation.
In Greece, an associate member of the E.C.M., price advantages of up to 8 per cent

These, then, are only some of the ways in which government has assisted in the E.C.M. countries.
May I ask the hon. lady a question? Would she indicate to the house in what period of time these inducements were given to industry, what year?

They have been given in various years since the beginning of the E.C.M. up to the present, and in different countries they have different periods of time relating to different industries.
In addition, this party has a program for regional recovery. We propose to set up an agency of the federal government which will be charged with the rehabilitation of problem areas. We of the Liberal party feel that to meet today's needs it is necessary to establish a Canadian standard of development opportunity. A new Liberal government will end1 the situation in which some Canadians have much poorer opportunities than others because they happen to live in areas whose resources have never been developed or whose industries are declining.
This agency will be responsible to one minister. It will identify the areas where a special thrust for development is needed, and suggest effective action programs. These programs will be examined with the provinces and the municipalities, with the industries concerned, with the federal departments and1 with local representatives. The programs will be backed by good administration, as well as by the necessary money.
Liberal action to meet the special requirements of development areas means capital grants for basic development projects such as roads, power generation and transmission, and other public investments. It means that private industry will be helped to get things moving, and in that regard tax incentives will be offered to companies which expand or modernize their operations, or which start new industries in the development areas. It means such things as federal public works programs. It means a municipal loan fund to provide capital for municipal works and services. It means that we will assist or aid in urban renewal and rural development and will make more capital available for clearing slums, for improving farmland, for reforestation, for development of recreational and tourist areas and for improving rural housing. Federal government purchases will help firms
	'

in the development areas, and the Liberal program for vocational training will be particularly designed to help workers displaced from declining industries so they can more easily move to new or expanding industries close to home.
In addition to all this a new Liberal government will provide an industrial development bank to operate as a vigorous agency for Canadian development. Another proposal which we have set forward is that dealing with urban redevelopment and the municipal loan fund, to which I have just made reference. A municipal loan fund is something which this country has long desired. It is understood by the Liberal party that one does deal from the federal government to the municipal governments, that they are the creatures of the provinces and must be dealt with through the provincial governments. However, our answer is to set up a municipal loan fund, and we believe that fund should be organized in consultation with the provinces and municipal representatives so that it will not conflict with existing sources of capital. It will provide loans for sound municipal improvements, of which provincial governments approve but for which capital is unobtainable at reasonable terms from existing Canadian sources. These loans will mean that municipalities can meet our great backlog of municipal requirements. They will create new jobs all across Canada and help to get our economy moving again on sound projects.
In so far as urban renewal and urban redevelopment are concerned, all hon. members know that many of our big cities need special development measures. They have slum areas where overcrowding and poor housing breed ill health, family tension, crime and juvenile delinquency; where perhaps adults now cannot live well and children cannot get a proper start on the road to good citizenship. We believe that no Canadian family should have to live in those conditions. We all suffer in health and amenities because of the pollution of city air and water supplies. Our surroundings are made ugly by urban blight. We believe we have to attack these evils, and a Liberal government will attack them and will work in co-operation with the provinces and urban municipalities.
In addition we have a full program for government planning. Now, before I hear any outcry about the use of such words, I hasten to add that such planning is the answer not on the basis of socialism but on the basis of co-operation between government and private enterprise. Mr. Pearson and the Liberal party have long recommended the establishment of an economic advisory council.
Mr. Graff fey: You are adopting all our policies.

We have the conviction that such a council should be composed of representatives of labour, industry, agriculture and government. The council's function would be to find out and analyse what is going on in the country; to study what is planned in all types of industry and in all the regions of Canada; to study such major problems as automation; to investigate economic trends; to publish outlook reports and, finally, to make recommendations to the government which in our system has, and must retain, the responsibility for policy and action.
The studies and reports prepared by the council would enable the government to secure a detailed and objective picture of the whole economy; to know its problems and its potential, and to assess its performance in the light of that knowledge. With such information the government would be in a better position to implement effective policies designed to reduce the gap between the potential and the actual performance of our economy. Private business would be in a position to use the targets and the forecasts prepared by the economic council for its own guidance. Government and business together would be able to take a reasoned view of our economic needs and the programs required to meet those needs. This would lead to better understanding and more effective co-ordination between the private and the public sectors of our economy.
A moment ago an hon. member said that what I was suggesting, an economic advisory council, was comparable to the national productive council which was set up last year. Nothing could be further from the truth. Some indication of that fact is that the United States has a national productivity council, yet the new President of the United States recently found it necessary to set up something very close to what the hon. member for Algoma East has been suggesting. That was a new economic council which is called the president's council of economic advisors. In the United States it was found necessary to have both, and of the two the more important has been the president's council. Just contrast the lethargic position of this government with the hustle of our neighbours in the United States.
I suggest that hon. members take a look at the periodical U.S. News and World Report of February 19 last, in which there is an article entitled "New Tools to Control Booms and Slumps". It contains the following:
Kennedy aides have been instructed to draw up a broad, new plan to control the economy. They have been told to use any and all devices to nudge, stimulate, goad, divert or restrict economic activities of all kinds.
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth
The chief planners are the president's council of economic advisers and a new staff of economic analysts and planners, just created in the treasury and directed by under secretary Roosa.
Some of the tools which are in use in the United States, which have been recommended by President Kennedy, include a bold use of the federal budget and the national debt to cut rates of income tax when a recession threatens, and a speed up of public spending when unemployment rises. The President has already asked congress for emergency powers to make temporary tax cuts, and for broad powers to ease trade negotiations with other countries. He has requested the establishment of a department of urban affairs to spend more than $4 billion a year for public housing, a federal mortgage program, community facilities and slum clearance, with plans to expand later to such fields as mass transport, education, air pollution control and water supplies.
That is the type of planning which we on this side mean when we say we have the answer. To those who think it has not been proven nor will it work let me quote from something which was said by probably one of the greatest of modern thinking Canadian planners and builders, the late Hon. C. D. Howe:
If our national development had been left entirely to private enterprise, Canada would not have attained its present status as a nation. And unless government continues to take a lead by well planned initiatives, guidance and regulation, it will not continue to develop as it should.
These, then, are Canada's wasted years. A stagnant economy is inexcusable for a country which possesses such great national resources together with a vibrant, forward looking people born to live in freedom. It is not necessary, and the people know that. A new Liberal government will provide the leadership, restore the confidence, and undertake the practical policies that will get the economy moving.
Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan):
That all the words after the word "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that immediate consideration should be given to the development of policies that would ensure an adequate rate of growth in the Canadian economy."

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If no one wishes to comment on the proposed amendment-I have in mind the form of the amendment-I will put it to the house.

It is
always a delight and a pleasure to listen to the sweet and mellow voice of the handsome and tender hearted lady member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh). However, I must say
1260	HOUSE OF
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth that we have some criticism to make of her proposals and, because she is such a nice lady, we are really sorry she is being misled on this question.
To illustrate the effect which this party has had on Canadian public opinion throughout the country, may I point out that the Conservatives are beginning to steal our slogans. They have already stolen one for the coming election, "Social justice for all". That has been our slogan for many, many years. Now the Liberals are beginning to steal our criticisms and even our language to some extent.
Even the hon. member for Assiniboia.

No, no. They do not steal in that case; they simply adopt. The Liberals are stealing our criticism and using our language, but they have not stolen our program. Do not let anyone be under any illusion in that respect.
Before I proceed to the main substance of my speech, perhaps I may say that speakers for an opposition group such as this must live in a certain atmosphere of anticipation concerning the amendment on the motion to go into supply. The hon. lady, in the course of her well delivered speech, said in the first instance that economic growth is essential for many reasons, hence it must be a major domestic issue in the coming election. We agree with that statement. It is true. That is our language. Then she said the Liberals have concrete plans to provide for such growth. We are waiting to see whether, later, members of the official opposition will be able to list any details of such plans so that we might know what they are.
Then the hon. lady said the Conservatives paint too rosy a picture. Well, we can agree on that. I am trying to indicate the things upon which we can agree in order to show how fair and unprejudiced we are. I may say that all my life I have found it very painful indeed to disagree with a lady, so hon. members can understand my situation this afternoon. Then the hon. lady said, apparently in an implied criticism of the wheat deals with China, that the government had committed itself to future deliveries of wheat to such an extent that we might not be able to make deliveries to our traditional markets. We in this group would not fear the possibility that we might not be able to make deliveries to our traditional markets. What we say is, let us stimulate production and let the farmers increase production so as to meet not only the demands of our traditional markets but the demands of all countries which desire our foodstuffs.


Further, the hon. lady went on to say we should need a million new jobs by 1965. I think we can all agree with that statement, so once again we are in accord. She made some comment about weeping and wailing over a lack of growth. I could not quite understand who the hon. member thought was doing the weeping and wailing. Certainly it was not any member of this group. We deplore conditions which are not satisfactory, but we do not weep and wail; we advance ideas and programs to try to improve the situation.
Since the founding of the New Democratic party the Liberal party has adopted so much of our program and vocabulary, as well as our parliamentary leader, that the Canadian people must wonder whether the Liberal party is altering its basic philosophy of ensuring, as a government, that big business maintains its unfettered control over our economy and arbitrarily dictates the standards of living of the people of Canada at the expense of consumers and producers.
We in this group base our policies on a few simple statements. We believe that every Canadian child, regardless of where that child may live or the economic situation of its parents, is entitled to all the education it is capable of receiving with advantage. We believe that every able bodied adult who is willing and able to work should have guaranteed employment. We believe that all the people of Canada should have protection against the hazards of illness or disease or accident of any kind or extent without their economic security or their savings or their future being imperilled. We believe that the country is responsible for the care of the disabled and for those who are unable to work on account of disability. We think they should be cared for at the expense of all of us and given security with a measure of comfort. We also believe that our older citizens should be able to enjoy their retirement with security and also with a measure of comfort.
Are you against sin?

I see that the hon. and active member for Brome-Missisquoi, where they raise ducks and, apparently, duckies, is interrupting me but it appears that at heart he is sympathetic to my views.
The Liberal party is attempting to convey the idea that it will provide planning in Canada. Hon. members will notice how popular this word "planning" has become. The Minister of Finance who, I notice, is listening attentively to my remarks, will remember that some years ago one or two

members got up in this house and said "Anyone who suggests planning suggests slavery". Well, we have come a long way since that day.
Finally, we are told that on February 20- not in this house but addressing the junior board of trade in Toronto-the leader of the Liberal party spoke at length and impressively in favour of action in both the private and public sectors in order to ensure the growth of our economy. But he had to reassure big business. He had to show big business that this was, after all, part of the electoral gimmick strategy, so he uttered the following words:
Planning, why? When economic action is taken in the public sector it should be designed primarily to stimulate and increase activity in the private sector.
I want you to notice this:
When economic action is taken in the public sector it should be designed primarily to stimulate and increase activity in the private sector.
When we quote these words we must remember that although we have over one half million unemployed in Canada at present, the balance sheets of large corporations indicate some have made the largest profits in their history under these circumstances. We are devoted to the principle of planning for the people under the direction of the people's representatives, not by big business and vested interests.
I return to the subject of the Leader of the Opposition, who has a fascination for me this afternoon. Later in his speech on this occasion he apparently felt he had not provided adequate reassurances, and from my point of view he attempted to correct the previous impression he had created of the rejection of his own party's policy of support of free enterprise. I quote the following from his recent and famous speech:
In this new world government and business must co-operate. Neither can afford to operate in a haphazard way. What we need now is careful co-operative planning. By this I do not mean planning, or a planned economy on a socialist model. A directed and controlled economy of that kind is for us not only undesirable, it is impossible. I mean planning, not with a view to bringing about more controls, but planning so that there can be a greater opportunity for profitable progress in the private sector of our economy.
When the hon. gentleman speaks I hope he will explain to the house that apparent contradiction in terms and objectives from the general impression created by his speech. If I remember correctly the speech was made to a board of trade in Toronto on February 20. You seldom find members of the cabinet or leading spokesmen of the official opposition addressing trade unions or farm organizations. Usually they address chambers of commerce,
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth boards of trade and groups of that kind, for which they have a natural affinity.
And the national farmers' union and the Saskatchewan farmers' union.

When the Leader of the Opposition hears what is being said by the national farmers' union concerning the expression of opposition to the principle of marketing boards on the part of hon. members of the Liberal party and those on the government side of the house, he will not wish to turn up at another farmers' meeting.
This is extraordinary. The Liberal party proclaims that the haphazard relationship of the past between big business and Liberal governments must now be organized, with the assistance of an advisory council, to plan for more profits for the private sector. This council would be in a position to use for its own guidance, to assist in its decisions, the targets and the forecasts prepared by the economic council.
Let me quote some other remarks attributed to the Leader of the Opposition. This group has been watching every word spoken by the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate. In fact we have a special man watching him for his pearls of wisdom.
The Ottawa Journal reported the Leader of the Opposition as saying in Hull on February 2 last:
The Liberal government would set Canada going again not through socialism but by planning to give incentive to private enterprise.
This sort of planning is compared by the hon. gentleman with that prevailing in Europe. But the Canadian people cannot be misled. The Liberal planning represents the theft of a word, not the acceptance of an ideal. I give the Leader of the Opposition credit for having honesty and integrity, and we all respect him, but he is addicted to the free enterprise doctrine. He is going to continue to plan for the people who have brought about every major war in history and caused every line of unemployed persons in every country of the world. If we leave it to them, in the future we will face a third world war.
How can we get our growth rate up to the necessary level? I will speak about our policy so there will be a clear understanding of what we stand for, without hemming or hawing. The New Democratic party maintains that Canada can only achieve and sustain a high rate of economic growth if she plans her economy to ensure the best allocation and use of her available resources and technology.
Canada has not had this kind of planning in the past. Whenever our growth rate has slowed down in the past, our government

Alleged Lack of Economic Growth has relied on natural forces to get it moving again, has subsidized private corporations to encourage them to undertake new investments, or has undertaken certain emergency government expenditures itself.
We give credit to the government for the introduction of such measures as the winter works program, but even that program would have been opposed by the old parties years ago. We all remember what happened in the hungry thirties, when few of the unemployed in Canada could avail themselves of a program of this nature but were offered 20 cents a day in relief camps. We have advanced since then. Since that time the C.C.F. has had an influence on Canadian public opinion, on the opinion of governments and official opposition leaders. No government today would dare return to the conditions of the thirties because of the change in public opinion.
What is a democratically planned economy? We say it is one in which the principal economic and social activities are co-ordinated and developed through deliberate planning by a democratically elected government. This should be contrasted to an unplanned economy where the principal decisions are made by private corporations and by powerful individuals associated with those corporations.
Let me illustrate that point. Last week I spoke to an important person in the Canadian pulp and paper industry. The industry faces an uncertain future. The present market absorbs approximately 90 per cent of the production of the mills in operation. This gentleman complained to me about the fact that another large mill is being contemplated to enter into production in the near future, when only 90 per cent of the present production is marketable. This seems to be the result of lack of planning and direction from the federal government in co-operation with provincial governments. That is what we mean by government control of industry, direction of investment and so on.
In our opinion a democratically planned economy is designed to serve the interests of the majority. An unplanned economy is designed to permit private corporations to pursue the goal of maximizing their profit. It is only by chance that what the private corporations do in pursuing this goal will be in the interests of the majority of the people. We must take the Leader of the Opposition at his own word. He intends to make it possible for private corporations and big business to increase their profits and expand their activities.

We believe the investment decisions of the various private corporations are unco-ordinated. Each corporation or group of corporations is concerned with its own sector of the economy and proceeds without concern for either (a) those other parts of the economy by which it does not think it is affected or (b) the country's over-all economic goals. The big corporation executive may get just as worried as anyone else when he reads in his financial paper that Canada has too little investment, or too much, or the wrong kind, but these considerations will not affect his own investment decisions for his own corporation. He will continue to make those decisions which best suit his own firm's economic welfare as he sees it. Yet there is no guarantee that what makes economic sense for a private corporation will still make economic sense for the country as a whole when all these private decisions are added up.
The result is that we get overinvestment in some parts of the economy, underinvestment in other parts. We get overinvestment in the country as a whole at some times, underinvestment at others. This is very damaging to the stability of our economy and to its steady rate of growth.
With democratic economic planning, such as that which we suggest, we can allocate our resources to serve the over-all economic goals of the country. This would level out the disastrous ups and downs that plague our economy, ensure that the economy produces what the people want it to produce, and enable us to maintain a high rate of economic growth and a low level of unemployment. The only unemployment which should exist in Canada is that caused temporarily by climatic conditions, where it would not be economic to transport workers from one area to another.

May I ask
the hon. gentleman a question?
Certainly.
Would he not include seasonal workers in that list?

These people are included in seasonal workers. They are persons that are put out of employment because of climatic conditions. To illustrate, may I say that in the district in which I live, any logging about the 3,000-foot level is usually ended by Christmas time, not because the companies are not operating or because there is no work to do but because the snow is too deep for economic operation. Hence quite frequently there is a lay-off of some men in January and February and possibly to March 15, until the snow lessens again.

What else, it may be asked, does economic planning involve from our point of view? Economic planning does not concern itself only with the allocation of investment as between private capital and social capital, but also within these two sectors. Planning and controlling investment within the social capital sector is relatively easy, because here the government can take direct action. For example, if the government finds that the housing program has gone ahead very quickly and is in danger of overinvestment, but that municipal services like water and sewage are lagging behind, it can shift some investment funds from the former use to the latter.
Planning and controlling investment within the private capital sector of the economy is less direct. "Indeed", some people may ask, "why do we need government planning in the private sector at all? Surely private businessmen know better than anybody else what are the best investments for their own enterprises." That is the attitude of the normal private business enterpriser.
It is true that a certain investment decision might be right for company A, another for company B and still another for company C, and so on. But when companies A, B, C and so on all across the country are making separate decisions about how to invest and what to produce, there is no guarantee that this will add up to economic sense for the country as a whole.
We make that point very strongly because there is evidence of it all over the country. I have seen it in my own lifetime. Men have started operations in a certain industry, particularly in the lumber industry. I refer to that industry because I have lived in the lumber country. They started up operations because they could get timber at that time, not looking to the future. They may find that some operations are not economic, and you have bankruptcies growing and so on, whereas if there had been some guidance, or some planning, even in the provincial sphere, we would have had sounder and longer term development. In an unplanned economy we have one corporation building an oil refinery here, another producing television sets there, another building a steel plant somewhere else, all according to how they view their own particular segments of the economy. But nobody puts all these programs of capital investment together in order to see whether they add up to a good program for the whole economy.
The other parties depend on some sort of invisible hand-the free market and so on- to see to it that this hodgepodge of private investment plans makes over-all economic sense. But there is no such invisible hand. There is no sort of over-all guiding hand in the economic field. All this in many cases
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth ends up with economic chaos because there has been no planning. There is no machinery working automatically in the private enterprise economy to see to it that our capital investment is neither too small nor too large and that it is growing in the most desirable places.
That is why we have periods of underinvestment and unemployment such as we are in now, and other periods of overinvestment and inflation as we had in 1955 and 1956. This is also why we have misuse of our investment capital with some sectors and regions being starved for needed social and private capital while others overinvest to the point that they have excess capacity for many years to come. That is not just a wild statement by radicals; that is a fact, and we find the results all through our economy in recent years.
Before my hon. friend leaves that point, I wonder whether he would permit me to ask him a question?
Yes.
I have been trying to follow what he is saying. Is he saying that there should be no private or corporate investment without government approval?

No, Mr. Speaker. We are talking about the commanding heights of the economy, those sectors of the economy which have a controlling influence on the economic destiny of the nation. As we have said before, we believe in public ownership wherever it is socially desirable and wherever it is indicated that it is in the best interests of the nation. We believe in much larger development of the co-operative enterprise. We believe there is a tremendous opportunity for socially desirable and socially responsible legitimate free enterprise, which is found largely in smaller industries, community industries and services, small businesses, farming and so on. In those sectors you will find economic organizations or groups themselves, under a change in our philosophy, directing their own destiny, working together co-operatively in accord with a national plan which has in mind the over-all planning we suggest. We believe there is a great amount that government can do by giving some direction and some guidance, some central purpose, to the development of our economy. In those large sectors we suggest planning as I have mentioned, and in these other sectors we suggest the influence of government, smaller group organization and co-operation to bring about the same result.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?

Yes.

Alleged Lack of Economic Growth
Is he suggesting that no new enterprise should commence without government consent or that no investment should be made without government consent?

I am not suggesting that no investment should be made. I will illustrate the matter in this way. I mentioned this large pulp mill that is going to be built. I do not know where it is going to be built, as a matter of fact, but I know it is going to be built. It will make more acute the problems of producers now in operation at this time. This is the situation in various segments of the economy including the mining industry, the forest industry and large scale manufacturing. We believe that government policies must be such that they will have the power to control the situation so that there is no uneconomic investment-
Would the federal government have that power?

Yes. It would have great influence on it through taxation and fiscal policies. We recognize that this is not an easy problem to solve. You will have to have the co-operation of provincial governments in many of these fields in order to reach the desired objective. But we believe we must start in this direction. We do not underestimate the difficulty, but we are laying out a positive program rather than let the economy drift, in our opinion, as a free enterprise economy in which large scale investors have no concern for the other sectors of the country except their own. I am not blaming them a bit, because under present circumstances they are forced into that position.
Mr. Speaker, I observe people nodding their heads and waving to me. I am just doubting whether my time has nearly expired. In any event I am going to say this. A New Democratic government would take steps to end what we term this economic chaos. This party has no faith in the invisible hand, as I said before. What planning machinery would a New Democratic government establish? A planning board would be set up, staffed with specialists in various fields, including economists, statisticians, engineers, scientists and so on. This planning board would follow four basic steps:
1.	Find out what the people want their economy to produce, and how they want it to perform.
2.	Find out what the economy is capable of doing, based on the available resources and technology.
3.	Set up a number of goals within the limits of the economy's capacity and based on the people's choices.
IMr. Herridge.]
4.	Draft a plan which would so allocate our resources and technology that these goals could be attained.
This plan would be presented to the cabinet who would discuss it and, after making any changes that they deemed necessary, would present it to parliament for debate. That is when the Minister without Portfolio would have his opportunity if he were here at that time. If parliament passed the proposals outlined in the plan, the government would proceed to put it into action.
There are many details of such a plan. Some might say, how would the planners find out what the people want? Other members of our group will go into the matter of how the planners find out what the economy is capable of doing and how they set up goals for the economy. Our people have these things worked out in considerable detail. The techniques of planning are rather complex but the general ideas involved are fairly simple. First of all, we have the spending and taxing powers of the government. This very general approach, of course, is not adequate in itself. Government spending and taxation must vary for different sectors of the economy and different industries. For example, corporation taxes can be made higher for industries that are overinvesting and lower for those that need to invest more. Government spending should be heavy in those sectors of the economy such as social capital and those regions like the maritimes that have difficulty attracting the necessary private investment funds. We say that Conservative, Liberal and Social Credit governments have not used their spending and taxing powers in this way to influence the direction of investment.
Then there is the question of the Bank of Canada and monetary policy. The proper policy to follow during periods of inflation is to contract the money supply, which raises the interest rates on loans made by chartered banks. This makes it more difficult for businesses to acquire funds and thus helps prevent them from overinvesting under the wrong circumstances and conditions. In periods of recession and unemployment the proper policy is to expand the money supply, which lowers the interest rates on loans made by the chartered banks. This will make it easier for business people, municipalities and home builders to borrow money for needed investment to stimulate the economy. Money, in other words, should be tight in periods of inflation-I do not really like the word "tight" but it is very hard to find another word to express the idea-and easy in periods of recession.

We hear people say, would planning mean regimentation and loss of freedom? The planning board which a C.C.F. national government would establish would not govern the country. Its role is to use its specialized training to gather information and draw up plans. The final authority will always be the people themselves through their representatives in parliament. All plans drawn up by the planners would have to receive the approval of the elected cabinet before being presented to parliament for debate. After being presented for debate the people's representatives in all parties would have full opportunity to discuss the plan, propose amendments, and reject or accept it. That is democratic enough, is it not? Moreover, economic planning does not mean directing or regulating every economic act or even any large number of acts.
I could go on to deal with the Bank of Canada and monetary policy, the control of finances and the necessity for a Canadian development fund which we believe would channel investment into uses which today are neglected by the private investor. We believe in the planning of public investment. There is a great opportunity for public ownership and there are other planning agencies that could be developed. There are several besides the ones I have mentiond that have been present for some time in the Canadian economy and which could be used in the over-all planning process. We could utilize them to greater advantage. I give as examples Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the board of transport commissioners, the wheat board, the restrictive trade practices commission and the tariff board plus a large number of provincial agencies whose cooperation we would seek to obtain in giving effect to a program which would provide a national economic purpose for our country. Today there is no attempt to co-ordinate the work of these agencies with a national economic plan. A New Democratic government would co-ordinate their activities just as it would co-ordinate the activities of big business.
I say in conclusion that in an unplanned economy people have very little say about how their economy is to perform, what it is to produce, and so on. The only way they can express their wishes in an unplanned economy is by their purchases in the market place and this only works to their advantage if the market place is perfectly competitive. I might say that there are fields in the smaller areas of business and industry where they are competitive. In fact, of course, the market place is controlled in general by a handful of
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth firms in each industry so that to a very large extent the people's wishes can be ignored.
Democratic economic planning would give the people as a whole a degree of control over their own economic destiny which they do not now enjoy. Instead of just hoping for full employment, rapid growth and security they could take positive steps and participate in the planning to see that the economy provides these things. Economic planning does not impose choice; it allows choice where little now exists. It offers an opportunity for people in all walks of life to co-operate with the national and provincial governments with some purpose. It will give purpose to their lives, a sense of security and a central direction to our economic development. It offers freedom to the Canadian people in the fullest sense of the word.
Mr. Speaker,-

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the past weeks and months and again today we have heard a number of misleading speeches and have read a number of misleading articles and publications put out by the Liberal opposition, all attempting in some strange fashion to convey to the people of Canada that this country's economy has slowed down. In fact, I think the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) used the word "stagnating" this afternoon. So, Mr. Speaker, we in the government welcome this opportunity to set the record right, and I should like to speak about the economy at this time under three headings. First of all, I should like to deal
12GB	HOUSE OF
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth with the situation which this government found existing in Canada when we took office in June, 1957. Then, I should like to deal with the progress that has been made since that time. Finally, I should like to deal with the prospects for the future.
First, I shall begin with what we found when we took office in June, 1957. Early in 1957 it was apparent that two important changes had taken place in the trading world. The first was that the countries of western Europe and Japan had completely recovered from the devastation of war and, having rebuilt their economies and their productive machinery, were no longer customers for many of the products we had been selling them in large quantities since the end of the war. The second change was that these countries, having replaced their productive machinery with the most modern and efficient equipment in the world, were rapidly becoming very serious competitors for our market both around the world and right here in Canada itself.
In addition to these two disturbing facts of economic life which we discovered when we took over the government in June, 1957, we also found that the Canadian economy had been for some months steadily slowing down due to the tight money policy imposed by the Liberal government of that day. Government economists had, early in 1957, warned that industrial activity in Canada was contracting at an alarming rate. The government's tight money policy had made it impossible for industry to acquire the funds necessary to invest in new plant and equipment and in new inventory which it needed, and the expansion of the economy had slowed down accordingly.
Now, Mr. Speaker, faced with such a situation we immediately set about the task of readjusting the economy to the conditions of 1957. As a result of the policies which were adopted, the country came through this difficult period of readjustment fully as well as the United States which faced similar problems. In fact, Mr. Speaker, because of the corrective measures which were adopted so promptly there was less of a let-down in industrial activity in Canada than there was in the United States. The final proof of the effectiveness of this government's actions during these difficult years is the fact that the Canadian economy is again moving vigorously ahead. So that all members may know just what has been accomplished during the present government's term of office, I should like to cite some key economic indicators, and in each case I will show the increase that took place between 1956, the last full year when a Liberal government held office, and 1961.
[Mr. Hees.l

In so far as total employment is concerned, total employment increased between 1956 and 1961 by no less than 452,000 new jobs, a percentage increase of 8 per cent. The gross national product increased by $6.8 billion or 22 per cent. Exports increased by $900 million or 19 per cent. Imports were kept down to an increase of $200 million or an increase of 3.5 per cent. Total personal income increased by $6.8 billion, an increase of 30 per cent. Labour income increased by $4.6 billion, an increase of 30 per cent. Corporate profits increased by $207 million, an increase of 6.2 per cent. Industrial production increased by 15 per cent and consumer spending increased by $5.8 billion, an increase of 30 per cent. Total personal savings increased by $400 million, an increase of 30 per cent.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that all hon. members, in fact all the people in the country, will agree that this performance, particularly when you take into consideration the very difficult conditions we faced when we took over the government in 1957, is a very creditable one indeed. However, Mr. Speaker, the most spectacular advance has taken place during the past year when the economy really started moving in high gear. I should like to give you some examples of just what has taken place during these past 12 months. The latest figures available in respect of export trade are for last November and we find that during the first 11 months of the year exports increased by 8 per cent over the first 11 months of the year before. This rate of increase was more than double the rate of increase for the last five years. During the last three months of that 11-month period, in other words last September, October and November, the rate of increase was 15 per cent over the same three months the year before. I think you will agree, Mr. Speaker, this indicates quite a remarkable rate of acceleration. First of all, you see a steady increase year by year and then during the past year double that rate of increase; and during the past three months the rate of increase was doubled again. This is acceleration if I ever saw it, Mr. Speaker.
During the first 11 months of the year we achieved a surplus trade balance of $27 million, the first surplus trade balance since 1952. In 1956, the last year of Liberal government, Canada had a trade deficit amounting to $713 million. So we see that during the past year we produced right here in Canada nearly three quarters of a billion dollars worth of goods which were formerly produced, under the Liberal government, outside of Canada and the production of which provided jobs for Canadians instead of for

workers in other countries. From November 1960 to November 1961, the last month for which figures are available, industrial production increased by 8 per cent. This was three times the rate of increase during the last five years, from the first to the third quarter of last year, that is within the brief period of six months, Canada's over-all production of goods and services in real terms rose by no less than 4.7 per cent. This rate of growth in national output exceeded that achieved in any like period in 14 of the last 15 years. I think everyone will agree that this has been quite a remarkable achievement under today's very competitive conditions. This growth has been achieved without any rise in the price level. In other words, not only is the present rate of growth of the Canadian economy comparable to any of the post-war years, but the absence of inflation indicates that it is proceeding on a sounder basis.
Between December 1960 and December 1961, employment increased by 180,000 new jobs. This was nearly double the rate of increase during the last five years. I should like also, Mr. Speaker, to cite some additional key indicators which are normally used to indicate industrial growth and which also demonstrate just where our economy has been moving during the past year. I will name the indicator, then the latest month in 1961 for which figures are available and then the percentage increase over the same month of the year before:	Manufacturing employment,
December, up 6 per cent; new orders in manufacturing, November, up 9 per cent; construction contract awards, December, up 15 per cent; production of motor vehicles, December, up 14 per cent; production of textiles, November, up 15 per cent; production of petroleum, November, up 32 per cent; production of nickel, November, up 28 per cent; production of steel ingots, probably the best key indicator of all, and this is basic steel, was up a remarkable 37 per cent.

In the kind of competitive world in which we find ourselves today nothing less than that kind of effort will do.
The important thing is to keep intact the present teamwork effort between industry and government. The Liberal opposition are making all kinds of extravagant promises in a desperate effort to regain power but remember, Mr. Speaker, they are the same people who slowed down the economy in 1957 with their tight money policy, and they can be counted on to apply the same tight money policy again if they should ever regain office, and slow down the economy the same as they did in late 1956 and early 1957. How ridiculous can you get?

It is vitally important that the present government should stay in control of the economy, and it is going to do just that. There is no doubt about it, and thus it will be able to maintain the present teamwork effort which is paying off in such a spectacular fashion today. Under this government, and with the

kind of co-operation we have had between industry and government, we can continue to work steadily forward towards full employment and the greatest prosperity this country has ever known.
That success story which I have just related to the house, that record of prosperity and that record of increasing employment is simply killing the Liberal opposition. Their plans have been completely upset. They have been desperately hoping for increased unemployment to help them in the next election, but instead of increasing unemployment they are being met with increasing employment and increasing prosperity, and so they have switched to a different tack.
