Mr. Speaker, the minister has made a brave effort to reassure himself and his supporters that all is well with the economy of Canada. He has cited figures which related to the past year and, more particularly to an upswing in the last quarter of last year, and has presented that as representing a picture of the economy throughout the whole period of four years, or more that this government has been in power.
The minister should know that figures for part of a year, even if they show a slight upswing, do not represent a sound economy any more than one swallow does not make a summer. Nothing that the minister has said can alter the fact that during the last four years and more during which this government has been in office the economy has expanded by only about 1.5 per cent per year as compared with 6 per cent per year in the previous five year period under the Liberal government.
My colleague the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) has already referred to this stagnation in our development and has spoken of the steps which a Liberal government would take to correct it. I should like to develop this theme a little further and in so doing I propose to confine my remarks to the position of the Atlantic provinces.
I think it was Lincoln who said that no nation could survive half slave and half free. I think it is equally correct to say that no nation can survive half rich and half poor. In the light of the present challenge to our democratic way of life perhaps we could go further and say that no society can survive half rich and half poor. We recognize the importance of the economic front in the war of ideas in which we are now engaged by
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth providing assistance to the under developed countries of the world. Surely we cannot afford to be less concerned about the underdeveloped parts of our own country.
Mention the provincial grants, then.

To speak of the Atlantic provinces as underdeveloped is not to say that no economic growth has taken place at all. But growth has been extremely small and painfully slow. At the time of confederation in 1867, the Atlantic provinces-perhaps I should more correctly say the maritime provinces- were relatively prosperous. They had flourishing economies based on agriculture, fishing, forestry, shipbuilding, shipping and international trade. Their provincial governments were in a generally sounder financial position at that time than the governments of the central provinces with a lower per capita public debt, a lower cost of living and a lower level of taxation.
One effect of confederation was to restrict this international trade which was an important factor in the maritime economy. The volume of trade with the central provinces which it was hoped would compensate for that loss did not materialize. The restriction of international trade produced, in turn, an adverse effect on the shipping industry and this, together with the advent of steam, crippled or curtailed the shipbuilding industry, though I believe at least one steamship was built in New Brunswick in the early days of steam. Thus, the Atlantic provinces were compelled to rely more and more on their primary industries of agriculture, fishing, mining and forestry as the basis of their economies. Ten years delay in building a railroad to link the maritimes with the central provinces and the overriding claims of military rather than economic considerations in determining the route of that railway were not conducive to the establishment of secondary industries. Consequently the maritime provinces began to lag behind the rest of Canada economically. This gap has steadily widened over the years. We can obtain a better idea of the magnitude of this lag by looking at the figures for population growth as published by the dominion bureau of statistics.
In 1871 the population of the maritime provinces, excluding Newfoundland, of course, was 768,000 representing 21 per cent of the population of Canada. Newfoundland had not entered confederation at that time. In 1961, 90 years later, the population of the Atlantic provinces, including Newfoundland, was only 1.9 million people representing 10.5 per cent of the population of Canada.

Without Newfoundland the population would be 1.4 million representing 8 per cent of the population of Canada. These figures show that in the 90 year period the population of the Atlantic provinces has barely doubled while the population of the rest of Canada has increased five times over. Had the population of the Atlantic provinces increased at the same rate as the population of the nation they would today have a population of approximately 4 million people. That represents a tremendous loss in terms of human resources as well as in terms of domestic market.
The most striking example is afforded by Prince Edward Island. In 1961 the population of Prince Edward Island was 103,000 people but 80 years earlier in 1881 it had a population of 109,000.
If we look at the figures for disposable income-that is income available for spending after the payment of taxes, etc.-the disparity is even more marked. As I said the Atlantic provinces today represent approximately 10.5 per cent of the Canadian population but they have only 7J per cent of Canada's disposable income. In my next comparison I shall use figures since 1949, the year Newfoundland entered confederation, so that province will be included. Personal income per person in the Atlantic provinces in 1949 was $622 per person compared with $982 per person for the rest of Canada. In 1959 the figure was $991 per person as compared with $1,546 per person for the rest of Canada.
Incidentally, the figure for Newfoundland has increased from $472 per person in 1949 to $841 per person in 1959 which indicates that Newfoundland is making some progress toward closing the gap between that province and the other Atlantic provinces.
It is not right to say federal governments in the past have been uninterested in this problem or that no attempt has been made to counteract it over the years. On the contrary a great deal has been done. No less than 14 royal commissions have been set up at various times to study different aspects of the problems connected with the economy of the Atlantic provinces. Out of the recommendations of these commissions have come such legislative items as trade subsidies, freight rate assistance, coal subventions, equalization grants, and the establishment of the industrial development bank, just to mention a few.
Nor do I wish to detract from what the present government has done by way of Atlantic provinces special grants, increased

subsidies and subventions for coal, small loans to business and other fiscal measures such as deferred depreciation. However, I maintain that this problem cannot be solved in a haphazard or piecemeal way by any number of isolated measures such as I have just mentioned.

In spite of the economic expansion referred to by the hon. members the economic gap between the Atlantic provinces and the rest of Canada is getting wider instead of narrowing as shown by the unemployment figures published by the dominion bureau of statistics.
In 1954 the work force of the Atlantic provinces numbered 501,000. In that year there were 33,000 people out of work the whole year round, on the average, representing 6.6 per cent of the work force. In 1956 there were 31,000 out of work the whole year out of a work force of 521,000, representing 6 per cent. Just wait. In 1960 there were 60,000 unemployed for the whole year out of a work force of 560,000 representing 11 per cent. To come to the latest figures which my hon. friend wants me to put on the record may I say this. The latest figures show that there are 84,000 people out of work in the maritimes-that is the last figure available and is for January 13-just exactly the same as the figure for the year previous, which was also 84,000. In other words, 14.7 per cent of the work force were out of work or unemployed on January 13 as compared with 14.9 per cent a year previous.
These figures do not tell the whole story as only 6,000 people joined the Atlantic provinces labour force between January of last year and January of this year. During the previous five years an average of 14,000 people had come into the labour force. If there had been a normal increase in the Atlantic province labour force of 14,000 people there would have been 84,000 plus 14,000 minus 6,000, or 92,000 people out of jobs on January 13. Between January 1957 and January 1962 unemployment increased by 5 per cent. However, the labour force increased by 12 per cent so that less than half of the new people coming into the labour force in the Atlantic provinces were able to find jobs. If this problem is ever to be solved, it must be done by special action on the part of the federal government. The provinces are powerless to do more than they are already doing until action is taken to remove the handicaps and disabilities under which they are now compelled to operate.

Reasonable people will understand that a situation which has been steadily worsening for over 80 years cannot be corrected overnight. Special treatment is required and special agencies must be set up to administer it. This solution must also be worked out within the framework of a national policy. It is foolish to pretend that this is going to be easy, and the effects of automation may render the solution even more difficult. It is obvious that if a region lags economically when the rest of the nation enjoys a boom, it is impossible to improve the economy of the backward region when the national economy is in a state of stagnation as has been the case during the past four years. The first step then must be to get the national economy rolling again.
In the past we have had a national policy nationally applied. The tax arrangements between the federal government and provincial governments which were pioneered by the Liberal party were aimed at making possible a Canadian standard of public services across the country. However, a national policy applied on a national scale cannot be adjusted with sufficient precision to take care of the great differences in economic conditions between the various economic regions of our country, because the instruments of control are too blunt to be adapted to the measures that must be taken. As a result, we have an overexpansion in one part of Canada while at the same time there is an underexpansion of the economy in another part.
I believe we must now go beyond aiming at a Canadian standard of public services and must aim at greater equality of employment opportunity. To achieve greater uniformity of economic development our national policy must be applied regionally instead of nationally. The national policy would set up the national goals for public and private sectors of our economy and then that policy would be applied in terms of regional goals for different economic areas. This may involve a new kind of budgeting procedure with the government presenting an over-all budget not for one year but for a period of say three years or even five years, with interim budgets brought in for essential adjustments. To implement this policy it would be necessary to set up, in my opinion, a new department of government, namely a ministry of regional development and rehabilitation. A regional development authority would also need to be set up to co-operate with industry, labour, and provincial and federal agencies in determining the best way of attaining the regional goals and to co-ordinate the efforts of all concerned so that the regional efforts can be integrated into the economy of the whole.

The development authority would have committees of experts to study and advise on the special problems connected with the resource industries of fisheries, agriculture, forestry and mining; the manufacturing industries and the marketing and transportation of our products.
I know that this sounds very much like planning, Mr. Speaker, and I have avoided using that word because the socialist party to our right seem to think they have a monopoly on it.

The socialist party in the corner. I listened the other night to the leader of the New Democratic party. A little later. I am very leery of questions. A Liberal government would set up a fund to provide industrial capital and capital grants for basic projects. A great deal has been said about capital grants and there is no doubt that they have a place in working out a solution to the economic ills of the Atlantic provinces. But any sound recovery must be based on our resources and it seems to me that a capital grants program could perhaps be most usefully employed to level out the imbalance between upsurges and downswings in the economy.
The co-operation of the chartered banks would have to be solicited with respect to the provision of credit, and I believe it would also be necessary to expand the industrial development bank to provide credit when for various reasons the chartered banks cannot conveniently supply it. In addition, there must be a system of tax and trade incentives.

To come back to the Atlantic provinces, I would point out that our economic problems resolve themselves into two parts. One is the employment gap and the other is the income gap. These will have to be treated as two separate problems and the employment gap should be tackled first. Any improvement in the employment gap will automatically be reflected in an improvement in the income gap.
In applying this regional policy we must start with what we have, our resources, including our fisheries, forests, mines, our agriculture, our tourist attractions, our hydro electric potential and our potential for secondary industries. We shall have to expand these and diversify our products and find new markets for them.
It seems to me that the provision of new markets or of expanded markets is really the key to any solution of the economic problems of the Atlantic provinces because our trouble can be traced directly to confederation which deprived us of our natural markets. At that time we sold nothing to the central provinces. Our trade flourished with the United States, England and other parts of the world but mainly with the United States. If, as our leader suggested, we can develop an association with other countries in an Atlantic free trade area, it seems to me that this would go a long way toward remedying the handicap from which the maritimes have suffered ever since they became part of Canada.
Some means will have to be found to induce manufacturing concerns to settle in the Atlantic provinces and to discourage Canadian firms from closing branches which they have in those provinces. All too often in the history of our region it has happened that somebody has started a little industry in a small way and when the industry has begun to flourish a firm from central Canada has come down to the maritimes, bought out the little industry and then closed it with the result that people have been put out of work. I think that sort of thing should be discouraged and in my opinion it can best be discouraged by providing tax incentives which would make it uneconomic to close down these small branches. They are not closed down because they are losing money or are unprofitable but are closed down in many cases because the companies concerned can make more money by doing so. This, of course, means hardship to the economy of the area affected.
I think we could also very well borrow an idea from Eire and some of the European countries and extend a tax rebate on profits derived from exports. That should encourage manufacturing industries from other countries to establish themselves in the Atlantic

provinces, and since these firms would already have their markets that problem would be taken care of.
The income gap, of course, is going to be much more difficult to close than the employment gap. With deference to the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), I would think that with a planned program over a period of ten years, or two five year programs it should be possible to close the employment gap fairly well. But I am not so optimistic about closing the income gap because even if we level out the rate of expansion it will be well nigh impossible for the Atlantic provinces to overcome the lead which the rest of Canada now has. Perhaps that problem will be taken care of some day by automation because there must come a time when production in the central provinces will level out and as automation becomes more common costs of production will be fairly well evened out as well.
If we can remove the handicaps of the extra cost of living and the additional transportation costs which now enter into our cost of production in the Atlantic provinces, I see no reason why the ingenuity of our people cannot make the economy of the area dynamic once more and do so not only to the benefit of themselves but to the benefit of the whole of Canada.

Hon. members opposite be they socialists or Liberals are advocating bureaucratic control, but their arguments are not always forceful. When I heard the new leader of that little group in the far corner of the chamber speak today in those terms of watered down socialism I said to myself, "Gone are the days of the fire and brimstone of the Regina manifesto". The hon. member for Niagara Falls said what was needed was an immediate stimulus

Alleged Lack of Economic Growth is an insult to the integrity of the civil service we have in Canada at the present time. Attempting to build in the minds of Canadians the concept and the fear that the state and the civil service is something which is necessarily evil and which must be avoided at all costs I feel is not doing a good service to the development of either the Canadian nation or the welfare of the Canadian people.
The Liberal amendment is one that, taken at its face value, could almost be agreed to by any political party in Canada. In effect all it calls for is an increase in the rate of economic growth in the country. I believe I have even heard members of the government admit that in the interests of resolving the problem of unemployment every effort should be made to increase the rate of economic development. The issue is not whether an increase in the growth rate is desirable; the issue is the manner in which we desire to increase the rate of economic growth.
I agree entirely with the hon. member for Niagara Falls who moved the amendment, that the problem of the growth of the economy is likely to be one, if not the major, election issue. The Prime Minister has told us in no uncertain terms that in his opinion the election issue is going to be free enterprise versus socialism, which to my mind is merely another way of saying very much the same thing as was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Niagara Falls about the potential election issue. However, we would be interested in discovering from either the Liberal or Conservative parties, or both, the manner in which they propose to increase the rate of economic expansion of our country.
According to my observations the Conservative remedy seems to be a patchwork of reforms and the instigation of economic activity through the winter works program, which is highly desirable and most beneficial, and vocational education, which is equally desirable if not much more so in the long run; but according to the observations of this group there appears to be no major or massive planning designed to give the whole economy of our country the lift that it so badly needs. As a matter of fact, in the main the Conservatives seem to reiterate the necessity of maintaining what they choose to call the free enterprise system but which in my books, having in mind the force that every government has and must necessarily have, is nothing more than the use of force to maintain the status quo. In my view this has always been expressed most neatly by simply saying that we live under a dog eat dog system wherein everyone to the maximum possible degree is allowed to do


exactly as he pleases, without regard to the public interest, and wherein there is really no genuinely free enterprise. It is very much controlled enterprise but controlled by corporations and powerful interests who are not necessarily held responsible for the public welfare as a whole. The Tories have yet to show that they have any intention of making the powerful economic interests in Canada raelly responsible to the over-all interests of the Canadian community.
We have lived through enough years of Liberal economic policy to recognize this debate for what it is. Yes, they will speak in the language of New Democratic policy but they will not dare to come out with specific remedies. They will not say by what method they will increase the tempo and the level of economic activity in our nation. The hon. member for Niagara Falls mentioned a few possibilities. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, she did not advocate that these remedies be applied in Canada, but she did hold up to us certain examples of what was happening in a number of other countries in the world. She mentioned tax concessions and tax exemptions. This reminded me of the tax free holidays granted to multimillion-dollar corporations, of which I have seen far too much in recent days, and which in the long run mean only the exploitation of resources and of people, with nothing left behind to show for it.
Is it the policy of the Liberal party to offer tax free holidays of five, 10, 20 or 30 years to exploiters so that they may come to Canada and give us work in order that our human resources can be applied to our natural resources? I think the Liberal party owes an explanation of what they mean when they speak of potential tax concessions, tax exemptions and reductions in taxation. Is this the catering to big business in which the Liberals indulged so liberally during their heyday in Canada? We know what it means in the long run. When corporations are given a free hand and every encouragement to invest here and to do as they please in our country, especially when non-Canadians are invited to do so, it means that we have an economy of boom and bust.
Under the circumstances existing in our country at the moment I am quite willing to concede that if the Liberals and Liberal candidates already nominated were to take the reins of office, unemployment possibly could be eliminated. However, I should like to ask them, how many unemployed will we have five or ten years hence when the long term efforts of their shortsighted policies make their influence felt? After the kind of

policies they are now advocating were enforced by the former Liberal administration, and they ran into a snag, they resorted to the remedy of confiscation of the savings of the people in that they deliberately permitted inflation to rob the hard-earned savings of ever so many Canadians, which has now brought about very serious additional problems in Canada.
If we want to increase production we must also consider the means by which we increase the level of economic activity in our nation. It is very hard for me to determine which comes first, the chicken or the egg, with reference to the financial structure prevailing within our country. I contend that an organized financial house, nationally speaking, is one of the major needs so as to increase national production. It is said that money is the root of all evil. An ordered financial house might be a great blessing at this time to the vast numbers of unemployed and to other Canadians who are in need.
If the government is looking for additional revenue in order to implement this objective, I would highly recommend that it reverse its present policy, begin to pursue a policy of the ultimate maximum production in which our people are able to engage and end its advice to various segments of the Canadian community to reduce production in order to maintain artificially high prices. To me such advice is not only immoral but in the long run I feel it is also harmful to the welfare of our people. The problems of Canadian agriculture, for example, will never be resolved by a policy of advising our farmers to reduce their levels of production if they want to maintain existing price levels.
If the government wants to put its financial house in order it ought to pay some attention to what is happening in the field of foreign investment in Canada. I am not necessarily opposed to Canada welcoming investment on the part of people living outside our borders. However, I find it a little difficult-and I do want to add this qualification-to understand how we can expect world peace in the long run if we, one of the wealthiest nations of the world, on balance are importers of capital. I believe we have a moral obligation to the development of peace and prosperity throughout the world to become, on balance, an exporter of capital instead of depending for our prosperity on an unfavourable balance in the matter of foreign investment.
We advocate the establishment of a federal investment board. If we want to have economic growth, we cannot afford to allow those who have investment capital at their disposal to invest it wherever it happens to please them, without regard to the investment needs 26207-1-82J
Alleged, Lack of Economic Growth of other segments of our society. I am very impressed by what is happening in a goodly number of other democratic nations in the world, where each year responsible officials assess the likely investment needs of their national government, of local governments, of quasi government agencies and of private enterprise. After assessing the likely national needs, they then get together and assess the possible investment capital that can be raised through the government and on the open money market. Then they arrive at an agreement, a compromise or an understanding, and in a number of cases the levels of government do not all run to New York to begin cutting each other's throat, begging the money-lenders in New York to buy their bonds.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps if the hon. member would tell us to what country he is referring.

I hope I will be able to hear the hon. member some other time. I understand that in the commonwealth of Australia there is an annual gathering of all three levels of government. They agree upon their essential investment needs, then the government of the commonwealth goes on the market and obtains this money, allocating it to the other levels of government. This kind of policy would save our municipal and provincial governments millions of dollars of needless interest. This is the kind of policy that our party would support. We believe we should go even beyond that, call in the private investment sector and act in consultation with it. I believe we must enlarge very greatly the role of the Bank of Canada in our nation.
At the time the Bank of Canada was originally conceived, our chartered banking system was the major source of capital within our country. Today, however, they are no longer the major source; they are very much the minor source. Even our credit union movement in Canada authorizes investments that are already close to one third of the volume involved in the operations of our chartered banks. Our insurance companies have powers vastly exceeding those of the chartered banks. I am not making a speech against the chartered banks. We have our central bank which is in constant consultation with the chartered banks. I believe the Bank of Canada is largely fulfilling the purpose, in this respect, for which it was originally designed. What I am saying now is that there are many other financial institutions operating on the Canadian scene whose operations largely offset the good intentions of our Bank of Canada in the monetary world. It is high time, as was advocated by Mr. Coyne in his controversial

Alleged Lack of Economic Growth report to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), that the minister considered the limitations under which the Bank of Canada has to operate at the moment. The former governor of the bank pointed out the other influences which had grown tremendously within recent years. I hope that the government will give very serious consideration to at least this aspect of the report of Mr. Coyne.
I hope that no one will assume, when I say that we must set our financial house in order, that either I or this party at any time advocates pressing the button to start the printing presses rolling. This would be against our basic principles. We believe that the amount of money in circulation is not only a matter of convenience but it has much to do with the bringing together of the human and natural resources; with the exchange of goods and with bringing in the purchasing power of those people who have been able to save, to the advantage of national development and employment. Many people will argue that when the last world war started the government very quickly found the money necessary. It ought to be obvious that we paid for that inflation, the inflation of our currency which was necessary for our participation in the war effort. The inflation of the savings of our people since the war has made us realize that to start the printing presses rolling, while it was urgently required at the time, was not helping to solve our problem in the long run.
We believe also that the government, to set its financial house in order, must return interest rates to at least the level they were when this government took office. I hope that some day financial experts will assess the tremendous cost to the Canadian people, in ever so many ways, of that deliberate increase in interest rates that was foisted upon the Canadian people and the Canadian economy. I hope they will be able to assess, with some reasonable accuracy, what the cost has been to the Canadian nation. I should like also to plead with the government to do everything it can and be at all times conscious of the need for it to remain completely sovereign over its monetary policy.
We are always willing to co-operate on the international level, but it is important, if a nation is going to be economically independent, that it also have complete control over its own monetary policy. I am not too sure that this has always been so in the past. As an aside to my remarks on finances, I should like to underline my opinion, expressed on other occasions, that before proper economic development in Canada can become a reality, we have to realize that our concept and structure of tariffs is completely outmoded.

There are only a limited number of nations in the world that have retained this government's attitude.
Now, I want to say one word about aid to the underdeveloped areas. I know a lot of Canadians will say, why not look after our own people first; charity begins at home, and the like. I would like to appeal to these people that aid to underdeveloped areas in Canada is the right thing to do, and we should do it primarily because it is the right thing. However, it is also very important for the maintenance of world peace, and particularly if we mean what we say, that we want to block the spread of communism, that we increase the level of our aid to underdeveloped areas. Apart from that major consideration, aid to underdeveloped areas will in very direct ways supply a boost to the Canadian economy and will supply employment for our people at home. When our manufacturing plants produce machinery that is used in Kenya or India then our workers have better chances of employment.
On this occasion Canadians are not going to be stampeded into a period of boom by Liberal policies of tax reduction and tax incentives, with ruthless exploitation of natural and human resources leading to increased foreign ownership and control, producing large surpluses and a depressed agriculture. As a socialist I am a conservative-with a small "c"-in this attitude, namely, that it is the height of irresponsibility to say "here are the people and they have the know-how; here are our tremendous natural resources; please come over and exploit us for our short term benefit and your profit".
The words "conservation" and "orderly development" are becoming ever increasingly important to the Canadian people. This time Canadians are not going to be stampeded by Tory hero worship, by high rates of interest, by financial concessions to the financial institutions, by more slick exploitation of national consciousness, by huge election war chests and the politics of sheer political expediency. This time a growing number of Canadian people will realize that if we are going to live as one happy family in Canada then we have to start behaving as members of a family. As members of one family we ought to be prepared to explore and assess our natural human resources. Then we shall have to decide on our needs and limitations, and how those human resources can best be applied to our natural resources so that the maximum number of our people will be able to enjoy employment and the social security they need so badly.

The federal government of Canada is the most powerful economic interest that the country has. We must recognize this, and we must also recognize that the government has a responsibility as to what happens to the economic destiny of our people. We must recognize that the people as a whole must decide to use this instrument of government that was designed for them out of the sacrifices of their forefathers. This instrument was designed for the people and the people must use it to determine their own economic destiny as they have hitherto been using it to determine their political destiny. I am therefore happy to support the amendment to the amendment proposed by my house leader.
Mr, R, C, Coates (Cumberland): I would have anticipated a more realistic approach on the part of the opposition to this first supply motion especially when one considers that most if not all the economic indicators of importance point to a strong upsurge in our economy. Instead we continue to hear the old tale of woe, the old tale that has come from that side of the house since 1957. Unfortunately they have been unable to separate their hopes from the realities of today.
I think all hon. members of the house remember the Templeton doctrine-high unemployment means good times for the Grits because they are in opposition. In fact that seems to be the underlying plan on the part of the opposition, and has been ever since 1957. Unfortunately for them this has not happened. Their predictions have not come true and they have not come true for a very good reason- because this government took the action that was needed to put our economy back on the road to success. If the Liberals do not soon remove themselves from this fools' paradise in which they live, then they will soon discover that the defeat of 1958 is only a taste of what they are going to get later this year.
It is a constant source of amazement to me to see hon. members from the Atlantic region, who were in this house before 1957, rise in their places and speak of doom and gloom in our economy when comparing our part of the country with the wealthier provinces in Canada without at the same time mentioning, even in a passing way, the many tremendous things that have been done by this government to lift our economy up and put us on the road to recovery, and to greater heights than we could have ever anticipated had we remained Liberal, with a Liberal government in office. One has almost to assume that they are not aware of the changes that have taken place. They, like the remainder of their party, also seek the solitude of this fools' paradise in which they choose to live.
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth
It must be that the members of the opposition from the Atlantic provinces have adopted the premise of "Maritime Gordon", one of their supporters who is presently preaching for a call he will never receive. He had a quick solution. The Liberals have been talking about shock treatments and he was going to give the Atlantic provinces a shock treatment. He was going to give that treatment to the people living there. He was going to give them one way tickets, straight out. This is separatism in reverse. Of course we in the Atlantic provinces know that Liberal thinking, when that party was in office, stopped short at the borders of Quebec. They never went beyond. We can all remember that former great Liberal prime minister, the Right Hon. Mackenzie King, saying "not one 5-cent piece for the maritime provinces." That is one promise they kept.

They sent them Pickersgill
instead.

It is appalling for any member from the Atlantic provinces to ignore the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants and his constituents should give him the treatment he deserves. I look forward to most of them receiving it. We blanked them in two provinces in the last election and it will be a complete sweep the next time if they continue the way they are now.
Whom are you trying to make happy?

Let me tell you, my friend, you won't be very happy when the next election is over. These Liberal representatives from the Atlantic provinces seem to have been brainwashed by this talk about gloom and doom. They don't even know what has been done, and for that reason I would like to put a few of the facts on the record, if they do not know them they may be able to read of them and appreciate them.
Like the digging of the Chignecto canal.

I have already mentioned the special adjustment grants-adjustment grants which will by March 31 of this year have poured $100 million into the Atlantic area. But we are not cut off at this point. We are not told: this is the end of it. No, Mr. Speaker, we are to get $175 millions more over the next five years. That is the type of treatment this government is giving to the Atlantic provinces.
As a representative from Nova Scotia I need go no further than my own constituency to see the tremendous growth in the economy that is apparent throughout the province.

In Springhill, for example?

Alleged Lack of Economic Growth Mr. Coates: All right. The hon. member mentioned Springhill and I am very happy he did so. Let us compare Springhill with the Pictou area which my hon. friend the present member for Pictou has done such an outstanding job of representing since he came to the House of Commons. I will tell you, my friends what you did for Pictou county. You closed coal mine after coal mine and the only solution you found was that offered by "Maritime Gordon"-move them out and give them one way tickets. That is your solution. Now let me say this: my hon. friend from Pictou county has worked, and his work is paying off. Almost every day we pick up a paper and see that something else is coming into Pictou county. Not long ago a new coastguard cutter went into the shipyards. Then, the other day there was a $2,300,000 car order. That is the type of representation the people of the maritime provinces have been looking for for years. If there had been a Liberal party in power in 1958 when this great disaster struck Springhill and took its only industry from it, leaving 7,000 people without an industry of any kind, there would have been a one way ticket for these 7,000 people. That would have been the Liberal solution to this problem. Instead, what has happened? The people of Springhill have four new industries. They have a minimum security penal institution. The Minister of Justice recently informed me that we were going to have a new medium security institution, the estimates for which were running as high as $2,500,000. This is an institution which would probably employ 125 people.
It does not stop there. This government, in co-operation with the government of Nova Scotia, has made available to the people of Springhill $450,000 in hospital grants so that they may build themselves a new million dollar hospital. Further, the Department of Public Works now has on its drawing boards a new federal building for the town of Springhill. In addition, Industrial Estates, a crown corporation set up by the Nova Scotia government under its great premier Bob Stanfield is prepared to investigate, and will investigate, every possible industry which can go into Springhill and into every other area of Nova Scotia. That is what was done for Springhill, since the hon. member asks, and let me tell him there will be more done as long as we have a Conservative government in Ottawa.
There are so many things that have been done for the Atlantic provinces that one does not really know where to begin or where to end. What I am trying to do is to put down a few of the things which I feel are of

real significance and which should be considered by some of the members of the opposition. If they did, then they, like some members of other parties, might begin walking across the floor as well.
We shall all be walking across shortly.

When they are so blind that they cannot see in front of them I guess we do not really want them; we can find better people ourselves.
Federal payments to Nova Scotia have more than doubled since 1957 from $31,336,000 to $67,928,000. Does this indicate the type of government the Liberals wish to provide? Our wages and salaries have notably increased. Our wage earners are receiving more than $1,500,000 a day every day, 365 days a year. In 1956 they received $440 million; the figure is now running at a rate of $593 million per year. For every $3 they received in 1956 they are now receiving $4. If hon. members want to look at it in another way, it took the wage earners 89 years to get up to $3 and only five years to get it up to $4. Is this the type of progress the opposition opposes?
Let us look at another field in which the opposition should have taken great strides in 1945-the field of vocational training. Hon. members opposite knew that we would be faced with this problem. It was all in the hidden report. But like so many other things that are distasteful, it was hidden away. Whenever there is something that does not fit in with their plans they put it on the shelf- they put it somewhere, where they cannot see it. In 1945 they should have been taking steps to see that the people of our country were trained so that when this technological advance came upon us our people would have been ready to step into the new jobs open for them. But they did nothing or next to nothing. In 1956 the Liberal government of that day paid its share of vocational training to the government of Nova Scotia. It amounted to $420,000. In 1961-62 that share will amount to $1,795,000 and next year, with vocational training schools under construction in every area of our province, it will be even greater Over the past six years the contribution of the federal government to vocational training has been $4,200,000. Of that amount the Liberal government provided ten per cent and we provided the other 90 per cent.
Let us turn to another promise, because the Liberal party is becoming a very promising party at the present time. Let us turn to hospital insurance. In 1919 the Liberal party promised the Canadian people that they were going to provide them with hospital insurance.
That is not correct.
I do not suppose it is.
The record was put straight the other day as the hon. gentleman knows.
The hon. member is always putting the record straight in order that it may please him.
I read the resolution.
Just forget the past.
I put the facts on record.

The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate wants to go back to the past. He is one of the very few members of that party who will undertake to do so. I do not think his leader agrees with him there, but then there are times when the four horsemen do not agree.
That is when we go to Quebec.
Under which flag?
That is what we would like to know. Which flag was it-Fleming or Dief-enbaker?

The hon. member will not get out of it so easily. One would assume that after what the Leader of the Opposition went through in the town of Amherst when being questioned about what has been described by some of his friends in the press gallery as a cocky, immature young man, he would have stopped talking about the flag, because he showed that day that if he could not handle that cocky immature young man, where would the Canadian people be if they put their faith in him as their leader?
With his faked report.
It only becomes vague when you start reading the facts.
Whose face was red?

I return to the subject of hospital insurance. I do not blame the opposition for not wanting to talk about this because they talked about it from 1919 until 1957 and did nothing about it. They did not provide a red cent to the Canadian people. As usual it was left to the Conservative government to fulfil the old promises of the former administration.
Hundreds of millions in hospital grants.

Now, now. The comments of hon. gentlemen opposite are somewhat like those of the Leader of the Opposition in the fog at Amherst. Hon. gentlemen opposite waver back and forth and straddle both sides of the fence. You never know where their
Alleged, Lack of Economic Growth feet are but you can always count on them being on both sides of the fence.
The late C. D. Howe said, "What's a million?"

It took a Conservative government to provide the people of Canada with hospital care. At this time this government is providing the people of Nova Scotia $1 million a month toward better hospital treatment.
We in Nova Scotia are very interested in education. We have a fine record in that regard. Let us look at university grants in which we are all interested. Hon. gentlemen opposite also choose to ignore university grants. In 1956 Nova Scotia universities received $695,000. In 1961-62 they are to receive $1,095,000 and this figure does not include the 50 cent per capita increase in the grant recently announced. Is this the type of aid hon. gentlemen opposite wish to overlook and about which we should forget? This is another example of what is being done for every Canadian from Nova Scotia to British Columbia by the present government.
Since my election in the House of Commons it has been my contention that the industrial development bank has not provided that degree of service to industries in the Atlantic provinces that should have been provided over the years. For a number of sessions I had on the order paper a bill which sought to amend the Industrial Development Bank Act to make its services more beneficial to industries in our area. As all hon. members are aware at the last session of parliament the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) amended the act in a very material way which had the effect of greatly broadening the scope of the measure. The financial resources of the bank were increased from $157 million to $400 million. It has only been a short time since the amendments came into effect but the results to date are most gratifying and indicate a far greater service to industries in the Atlantic provinces than could have been possible without the amendments.
An example of the effect this is having at the present time on business in the province of Nova Scotia alone is indicated in the annual report of the bank which reveals that 49 loans were made available to business in Nova Scotia last year as compared with seven loans made in 1956, the last year during which Liberals were in office. Seven times as many loans were made available in 1961 as in 1956.
An indication of the increased scope of the services of the industrial development bank is to be seen in the 1961 report of the president where it is stated that there has been an 84 per cent increase in the number of loans

Alleged Lack of Economic Growth made available under the act during 1961. This increase is far greater than in any previous year. Indeed, 23 per cent of all the loans made since 1944 were made in 1961. Ten new branches have been established since 1959 and in 1961 St. John's, Newfoundland, saw a branch established to serve that province thereby providing greater service to the Atlantic area.
An indication of the increased advantage being taken by industries and businessmen in the province of Nova Scotia can be gleaned from the report. In 1956 there were seven loans approved for a total amount of $393,000. In 1961 there were 49 loans approved, seven times as many as in 1956, for a total of $2,130,000. The increase in the number of loans is reflected in the increase in dollar volume of the loans.
This has been the story right across Canada with 1956 having seen 349 loans approved as compared with 1,364 in 1961, and almost double the amount made available to businessmen of this country between the period 1956 and 1961. As I pointed out, these amendments were not in effect for the full period of the fiscal year 1961. I look forward with confidence to the 1962 report of this bank as even greater evidence of the assistance that is now available to business as a result of the amendments and increased financial resources.
My hon. friend asked me about Springhill. I think it is only fair to point out what has been done in the rest of Cumberland county as an example of what is happening in every constituency in Nova Scotia.
Hon. gentlemen opposite speak about the economy not moving forward fast enough. I do not know how fast they wanted it to move but I do know that they had better start moving a little faster with respect to looking at the facts if they want to be around to see how fast the economy will move in the next four years.
There has never been a time in my memory when things have been as progressive and employment as high in Amherst as at this time. Every major industry in the town is expanding operations. Only today I received a letter from one of the large industries there asking me to see if I could obtain harbour and wharf improvements in a specific area as they are about to enter the export market no doubt due to the splendid efforts of the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) in the attitude he has taken toward uplifting our export trade.
Hear, hear.
The minister is applauding himself.
I did not hear the hon. member's statement. I merely knew it was a wise comment and applauded on that basis.
This is not the first time the minister has applauded himself.
I am much too embarrassed and overwhelmed with shyness to applaud.

Robb Engineering, the oldest major industry in Amherst, has been carrying out a constant expansion and remodelling of its facilities. At Pugwash a $2 million rock salt refinery operation will be added to the $3 million plant already in existence in that community. Last year a step forward was taken by this company in exporting its products to the United States for the first time.
One can go to Oxford and see the establishment there of a new factory by Industrial Estates Limited and their ability to secure federal contracts for the first time of a magnitude that was not ever possible previously. One can go to Parrsboro and see the ships loading pulp and lumber, in January, something which I do not believe the residents have seen for years and years. What is the reason for this activity? The reason is that the Department of Public Works has provided them with the most up to date facilities. One can go to the little village of Port Greville and see the shipbuilding industry throbbing, growing and wishing there was more room so that they could build more ships as a result of the forward looking program put forward by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) with his new subsidies.
This is the type of downcast, depressed economy that our friends opposite like to talk about. As I said before, Mr. Speaker, they are living in a fools' paradise out of which they had better come very fast. Otherwise, instead of worrying about who is going to be their next leader, they will all be sitting on the outside looking in at whomever the remainder of them, if there are any, try to choose for a leader.

Mr. Speaker, I was greatly surprised to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce today say that the former government gave business and industry no co-operation. He said they were receiving a great deal of co-operation now. By implication he meant that they received no co-operation from the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe. This is the most ridiculous statement I have heard since I have come to the House of Commons. I will say that Mr. C. D. Howe co-operated very well indeed as minister. He contributed a great deal to the development of this country. If my memory serves me rightly the Prime Minister paid

his respects to him and said so at the time of Mr. Howe's death. Hence the Minister of Trade and Commerce is at variance with his own leader.
It is not the first time.
As for myself, I think the minister has become so inflated with his own ego that he thinks he surpasses Mr. Howe in his value to Canada.
I was not comparing myself with Mr. Howe. I was comparing the department today with the department then.
Just puffed up by your own hot air.
I do not mind it one bit if the minister wishes to build himself up. However, I do not think he should do so at the expense of the good name of Mr. Howe.
Oh, no. We do not do that over here.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce painted a very rosy picture. He gave some figures. He gave percentage figures. I heard one Conservative member making reference to those on this side of the chamber and saying that we always referred to percentages and not to actual figures, As a matter of fact, I could give him some actual figures in connection with trade and commerce. I could give him the outright figure of the increase in business failures in Canada and the increase of the deficit of the C.N.R. under this government. They are not percentage figures. After listening to the minister I wondered why there was not a labour shortage in Canada at the present time-
The same old blue ruin.

-why at this time anyone was unemployed and why the unemployment insurance fund is still going down. The minister referred to the wonderful team work in his party. I will refer to some of that wonderful team work and where it has landed Canada at this time.
I think nobody will deny that there has been a slowdown in our economy from 1957 onward. The average annual increase in the gross national product from 1950 to 1956 was 6 per cent and since that time it has gone ahead only at the rate of 1J per cent.
That is not correct.
Then the bureau of statistics is wrong.

It is correct. In 1956, compared with 1950, the volume of national production on a per capita basis increased by
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth 22 per cent between those two years and from 1956 to 1961, it has gone down by 4 per cent.
That is not correct.
These are dominion bureau of statistics figures published by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
How ridiculous can you get?

speechtext: Order. The hon. member who started this last series of interruptions will very shortly have an opportunity to give his own version of the facts. In the meantime, I think it is only fair that the hon. member who has the floor should have it to himself.

The total capital expenditures in Canada in constant dollars increased by 62 per cent from 1950 to 1957, and there has been a decrease in 1961 from 1957. What is more important still is the fact that business capital expenditures are down by about 25 per cent. It is true that we have an increase in building, housing and some other sectors of our economy.
Of course, that does not count.

However, in the business sector, the figure is down by 25 per cent. Prior to 1956, unemployment was slightly under 3 per cent. Since 1957 it has practically always exceeded 6 per cent. We know that in February, 1961, we had the highest unemployment since the war when it reached the figure of 719,000. Unemployment is not down so much now when you take into consideration the increased number of people who are on direct relief. In some of the papers I saw it referred to as a 14 per cent increase and in some others as 17 per cent. Then you must take into consideration the number of unemployed in the vocational training program and in the civil defence forces.
And the number going to the United States.
Name the paper.

I think our trade is an important matter because trade accounts for about 25 per cent of our labour force. I am glad to note that we have had an increase in trade during this last year. However, 50 per cent of that trade in the first nine months of the year was due to an increase in shipments to communist countries. This is a trade diversion on which we cannot always count. I am also glad to note that we are shipping some commodities to Cuba. I have here U.S. News and World Report for February 26, 1962. In it there is an article which

Alleged Lack of Economic Growth is headed, "How Canada Helps Keep Castro Going" and which reads in part as follows:
At a time when the U.S. is appealing for support in a campaign to isolate Castro, Canada's exports to Red Cuba have reached record levels.
Food, machinery, aircraft engines and other goods from Canada-even explosives-are being used by Cuba's communist masters to stave off any internal crisis that might spark an uprising.
Chemicals, chemical specialities and explosives reached an export value of $600,000 while aircraft engines and parts totalled $169,000. Then the article goes on to say:

As one member of the House of Commons I would appeal to the government to stop shipping explosives and aircraft engines and parts to Cuba.

speechtext: Order. I am a Httle puzzled to determine how the present argument of the hon. member relates to the amendment and subamendment before the house.

Mr. Speaker, the new trade blocs present us with a challenge and I think we should investigate those blocs. I certainly do not think that at Accra the ministers investigated the European common market properly. For instance, the Minister of Finance said something to the effect that Britain would be on a slippery slope if she joined the common market. I have not got the exact words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce but they were to the effect that Britain would have to choose between the commonwealth and the European common market.
A Senate committee has stated that in the next five years or in the early 60's Canada will need to provide about one million jobs, and I do not think we can do that if our economy is standing still. If our economy had progressed at the same rate as it did in previous years under the former administration there would have been an increase in the gross national product of $14 billion in the last four and a half years. In goods and services this amounts to about $3,000 for the head of every family in Canada.
I have heard some reference to elections past and future, and the Conservative party won the last election largely on a vision. I was glad to hear one hon. member say tonight that his party would go to the country on its record. I do not propose to put on Hansard the platform of our party. The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) suggested tonight that we should have a reasonable and sensible alternative. I would say to him that


it is important to our economy above everything else that we should have a good stable and solid government, that we should have a sound fiscal, monetary and foreign exchange policy that will restore confidence among our people and among people of other nations.
The policy we have now discourages investment in our country. It discourages the building of new plants where people might be employed. I think this is very important to our economy. The policy that we have now produces a flight from the Canadian dollar. I predicted in the House of Commons last August and also in the previous year that unless there was some change in our fiscal and monetary policy we would have a flight from the Canadian dollar. I do not think that anybody will disagree with the fact that there is a considerable flight from the Canadian dollar at the present time. We only have to refer to Barron's Weekly, a financial magazine, which had this to say in this week's issue:
For more than four years then, Canada's Conservatives, adopting one misguided economic and fiscal policy after another, have been playing with fire.
Further on it says:
Canada's financial crisis worsens under this kind of irresponsibility.
I know there have been some articles in the press disagreeing with what Barron's has said but I can quote worse comments. Their comment is mild compared with those which appeared in the Monetary Times of London, in the New York Times some time last year and also in the London Spectator. Certainly in some of our own newspapers we have seen far worse comments than that which appeared recently in Barron's Weekly.
How can there be confidence, Mr. Speaker; how can there be new investment in the face of the present type of monetary and fiscal policy? Without new investment how can we expect to have any substantial upswing in our economy and in our gross national product? Without new investment how can we expect any great increase in employment?
In my opinion monetary policy is vital to our economy and to the welfare of Canadians generally. I know that at the time the minister announced a planned devaluation of the dollar I said that after this had been accomplished it would not be hard to maintain because of the way he set out to bring it about. In the budget debate I said at that time that it would create a lack of confidence and that this would be a strong psychological factor in depressing our dollar. What happened? We spent millions of dollars to depress the dollar and now we are spending millions of dollars to support it.

I will enumerate eight events, any one of which might have a considerable effect on our economy because of their effect through investment channels.
Number 1. In last May and June we had the Coyne affair which resulted in a bad press both at home and abroad. I think this was a psychological depressant on our economy and on our dollar, the results of which did not develop immediately.
Number 2. Then in June we had the long delayed budget and at that time the Minister of Finance made a complete flip-flop. He turned around and tried to depress the value of our dollar. If we turn to page 2673 of Hansard for March 31, 1960, we see that the minister said:
An attempt by the government artificially to lower the external price of the Canadian dollar would involve borrowing or raising by taxes very large sums of money with which to buy up foreign exchange.
Then, a little farther along he said:
In other words, we would be embarking upon a gigantic financial speculation with no assurance of success.
What success have we had? I know that already we are putting up $7 million a day to support that dollar.

How do you
know that?

I can read, and that is contained in the report of the Bank of Canada.
Number 3. In December, we had the reported firing of the Minister of Finance. I do not care whether or not there is any substance in the story; that is not the point. The point is that the Prime Minister allowed these stories to continue for two or three weeks without denying them. I think, myself, that created a lot of misgiving in the country. It is very significant that immediately after that we had to support our dollar, while immediately before that we were trying to suppress our dollar. We have spent $200 million since that time, according to the last report, supporting the Canadian dollar and trying to keep it from going lower. I think that is very significant.
Up to that time, it had been reported in the house we were spending money to keep the dollar down, and after that we were spending money to support the dollar. This split in the cabinet, I think, was very disturbing to the country. I am not trying to say that the Minister of Finance was to be fired; that is not the point. The point is that the story got out to the people of Canada, to the people abroad. It may have seemed funny on the surface, but it was not funny to the taxpayer
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth because, according to the last report, he has been paying up to $200 million to support that dollar.
In so far as the exchange rate is concerned, I may say that I saw a very funny cartoon. It showed the Minister of Finance holding a bear by the tail. He was in a very precarious position. I suggest the artist might more properly have shown the minister throwing the taxpayers to the wolves.
Number 4. In November I was in Ottawa and I saw a story in the Ottawa Journal to the effect that experts from the international monetary fund were coming to Ottawa to try to assess our troubles in connection with the exchange fund.
Number 5. Last year, particularly since last June, we have been debasing our currency at the rate of between $5 million and $6 million a day, that is up until early January. I do not know what has happened since then. We only have to go back a short time to ascertain what the Minister of Finance had to say about inflation. This is inflation because, in one year, we have increased the money supply by $1.2 billion, whereas to finance a boom year in years gone by, it has cost us between $400 million and $500 million.
The Minister of Finance had this to say on March 31 last, as reported on page 2673 of Hansard:
Let us give no quarter to such a defeatist attitude. Inflation acts like a drug on the economic system- even small doses breed a craving for more.
Then, farther along he said:
One of the most serious effects of inflation is that, like other drugs, it erodes stamina and willpower.
Are we to take it from this that the stamina and willpower of the government have been eroded?
Where is the inflation?
Would the hon. member not say that the printing of between $5 million and $6 million a day is not inflation?
It depends on the amount of goods being produced.

Then: Number 6. About a week or two ago practically all the members of the press, radio and television were saying that Canada would be on the carpet because of her actions with the exchange fund.
Number 7. The press also carried stories to the effect that Canada requested the meeting be in secret.
Number 8. At the Accra conference in September the comments that were made by our minister tended to create some doubt as to the future of the British commonwealth. We all had knowledge of the Coyne affair and of the

Alleged Lack of Economic Growth planned devaluation of the dollar. We also have knowledge of the inflation that is taking place. However, I cannot believe that the other items originated in the minds of the members of the press and in their minds alone as the government would like us to believe.
What does this all add up to? If you take any one of these eight items, along with our high rate of unemployment, the slow pick-up in our economy and our huge budgetary deficit, you have enough to affect the price of our dollar and to scare investors away from our country. You also have enough to scare the Canadian people from investing in different projects within this country. When you consider all these points together, it is no wonder that financial men in New York and Chicago are saying that our dollar will sell at 90 cents. The actions of the government have certainly brought about a lack of confidence at home and abroad. Confidence is one thing you cannot buy with dollars alone. This is something the Minister of Finance must get out of his head. I think you have to have stability. In years gone by our financial system was the envy of the world. Our foreign dealings were above reproach. If you read some of the press reports today, you find that is not the case. I say that the market for dollars is the same as the market for anything else. It will react more to uncertainties than it will to realities. I think our government is providing the uncertainties.
Now, the fiscal and monetary policies should be closely related in order to have a good economy in Canada. I will not go into the details of the conversion loan, but I will mention it in passing because the series of events set in motion by that conversion loan have carried us to the point where we have had to adopt our present fiscal and monetary policies a part of which has been the present policy of supporting our exchange rate. I will say also in passing that the conversion loan is the basic reason, after all, for the governor of the Bank of Canada appearing in Washington last week to defend the actions of this country in connection with the exchange rate. I can say that we gave the people a good economy, good employment, reasonable interest rates and hope for the future and I suggest that the people know the party opposite for their promises. They promised almost anything from an increase in the price of asparagus to a covered city in the north, built on stilts. I suggest that the people will know them for their works, our poor economy, high unemployment and poor hope for the future.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has been part of that team. He likes to refer to himself as part of the team, but I suggest


that team has produced some great records which have had something to do with the poor state of our economy. For instance, dealing first with the conversion loan I would suggest that probably the whole team got in on that decision. We were told that the conversion loan was the greatest financial transaction in Canadian history. Probably there is no doubt but that it was the greatest. Another record set by this government was the 719,000 unemployed last February. Another record was our bonds being sold at the lowest price in the western world, less than Cuba's bonds in the early days of the Castro revolution.
The other night I placed on the record the great increase in failures in small businesses and small industries. We have an economy which is standing still, but if there is any slight pick up in the economy from one month to another then a Conservative member seizes upon it with glee and tells us about it in the house.

And you
don't like it.
Then we have the high interest rates. When this government took over the average interest on all debt was 2.98 per cent, but now the Minister of Finance never tells us where it stands.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: He told you today.
Not the average interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes, he did.
He told us the average interest on some part of the debt.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: He told you the average interest on all parts of the debt.

This is the sort of thing that happens because of the monotonous overdraft of $2 million a day and as a result of the depletion of the unemployment insurance fund. That has to be added to it. It is little wonder then that foreign papers like the London Monetary Times and New York papers refer to Canada as having an economy that is in a mess.
I heard one speaker say tonight that Canada's prestige was high in all parts of the world. Well, I have been in Europe and I got the impression that our prestige was never lower.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Ridiculous.
Where did you go?

I will tell hon. gentlemen opposite that the information I got was unsolicited. When I presented a Canadian $5 bill they would not take it at the airport in

Lisbon whereas they said they took money from practically every other country in the world. They took Italian lira, they took money from some of the African colonies, from Brazil, from France, but they would not take Canadian money.
This government has offended Britain. It has offended the United States, Uruguay and British Guiana. We heard that in this house, and I do not think there is any doubt about it. It does not matter how often hon. members opposite get up and say we are on the wrong track. They say we have nothing to offer. The one thing we always offered, and still do, is stable and sound government, and that is something Canada has not got today. That is something we could always offer.

This constant reiteration of doleful facts, of doom and gloom from the Liberal party, gives me a pain in the neck. I do not want to embark on that subject right now as I would like to start tomorrow, if I may call it ten o'clock.

I don't think so.
Business of the House

I shall deal first with the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Niagara Falls. We heard from her tonight that the gross national product has gone up 1.5 per cent; from the last speaker, the hon. member for Welland, we heard it has gone down 4 per cent. It is probably written on the record that the Leader of the Opposition turned around and said "That is correct, look it up in the dominion bureau of statistics." The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate turned around and nodded his head saying "Yeah, man, that is right." All I have to say to all hon. members is that all they have to do is look up the record because the dominion bureau of statistics shows otherwise.
May I call it ten o'clock?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this debate will continue tomorrow.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, February 27, 1962
